### Parked windows Safari restored after a quit (2026-11-07)

- **What was seen:** after quitting and reopening Safari, the windows Margin had parked (the other profiles' windows of earlier switches) came back as small windowed windows on the Desktop, beside the one in use, in full screen.
- **Why.** A parked window is alive and normal, only out of sight. Safari saves and restores every window it has. Margin's quit closes parked windows (§13.1), Safari's quit doesn't, and parked.json re-parks only windows of the same Safari process (a Margin restart).
- **Now.** The copy remembers each window the app parks by its tabs' Margin ids (storage.local `parkedWindows`, ids only: `background/parked-restore.js`). It's dropped when the app un-parks the window, not when a link goes. In the copy's first minute, a live window is taken for a record whose window is gone only if all its tabs are the record's, at least half of the record's tabs are back in it, and no other window qualifies (`shared/parked-restore.js`). That window is marked `wasParked` on its entry. The app closes it through its copy, once (`Shell.closeRestoredParked`), and its tabs stay in their spaces, not open. It isn't closed if the app has it parked now (a Margin update keeps parked windows alive) or if it's in full screen. After the first minute, records of windows that are gone are dropped, so a window the person reopens later is never closed.
- **Tests:** `parked-restore.test.js` (the matching: exact, too few back, a foreign tab, two candidates, still open), `parked-restore-bg.test.js` (remembered, kept through a link going, known after a "relaunch", told once, dropped after the first minute), `window-tests.swift` `restoredParked`, `e2e-profiles.swift` step 9 (a restored one closed by its copy once, a parked one left alone).
- **Not yet:** the restored windows show on the Desktop for the second or two until their copy has matched its tabs. Hiding them sooner would mean guessing by size and place, which could hide one of the person's own windows.

### Parked windows closed before Safari quits (2026-11-07)

- **Reported:** closing the restored windows after Safari brings them back "feels very inefficient … we should close all the hidden … windows when Safari quits".
- **⌘Q and ⌥⌘Q** (Quit, Quit and Keep Windows) are Margin's first while a linked browser is in front with windows Margin has parked: hot keys in `AppShortcuts`' quit guard, apart from Margin's own keys and held by their own rule (`Shell.guardsQuit`). Never held otherwise, so with nothing parked ⌘Q is the browser's as it always was. On a press (`Shell.quitBrowser`), the guard lets go and every parked window is closed by its own copy (`ParkingRegistry.endAll` with the copies' closer, as Margin's own quit does; at most 0.6 s). Then the same keys are posted to the browser's process (`Shell.postQuitKeys`, `CGEvent.postToPid`; if that can't be done, a plain quit is asked), so Safari quits as it would have, its own "quit with these tabs?" included. If that quit is cancelled, the guard is held again after 2 s while windows are parked.
- **Logging out, restarting, shutting down** (`NSWorkspace.willPowerOffNotification`): the parked windows are closed the same way before macOS asks the browser to quit.
- **Not caught beforehand:** a crash, or a quit from the Dock or the Safari menu with the mouse (no app is told before). Those are left to the restored-window cleanup above, which stays.
- **Tests:** `tests.swift` (the guard's rule, its keys held apart from Margin's, which press keeps windows, let go), `e2e-profiles.swift` step 10 (⌘Q with a window parked: closed by its copy, then ⌘Q passed on once). The final quit check now asserts every window parked at Margin's quit is closed by its copy, rather than window 9 by name.

### Pages that set `<html>`'s overflow-x: scrolling in the box (2026-11-07)

- **Reported:** msu.edu couldn't be scrolled at all; on youtube.com things didn't load (the sidebar, more videos on scroll, a video saying the connection was lost until a reload). The request: a generic fix.
- **msu.edu, the cause:** the page says `html { overflow-x: hidden }` and `body { overflow: hidden }`. The box's weightless `:where(html) { overflow: clip }` meets the page's x value, and CSS turns a `clip` beside `hidden` into `hidden`, so `<html>` computes `hidden` up and down. `checkLocks` (content/page/box.js) reads that as the page locking `<html>` and leaves `<body>`'s own `overflow: hidden`. In the box `<body>` is the scroller, so nothing scrolls. Without Margin, `<html>` is `hidden`/`auto` and the window scrolls.
- **The fix:** `<html>` still clips both ways when the page says nothing sideways. While the page says `<html>`'s overflow-x itself (computed `hidden`, `auto` or `scroll`), the box clips only sideways (`boxCss(…, clipY)`), so what the page says up and down shows: nothing said reads `auto`, and `<body>` scrolls (the `side()` rule already makes it `auto` then). A page that really sets `overflow: hidden` on `<html>` still reads `hidden` and stays locked. The rule changes only when the page sets or drops its value (one layout of `<html>`), not at every check.
- **Not clip sideways only everywhere** (tried first): with `<html>` `visible` up and down, the window itself could scroll, and in a quirks-mode page WebKit makes `<body>` the document's scrolling element, so `<body>`'s sizes read as the window's (WebKit host `read-shape` W, a `document.write` of a page with no doctype: `<body>` 1200 wide in a 932 box).
- **YouTube:** not reproduced in the WebKit host with Safari's user agent: the search page's infinite scroll loads the same boxed as bare (19 → 77 results). A retest is asked for after this install and a reload; pages open across today's many reinstalls are a likely cause.
- **Tests:** `page-css.test.js` (both forms of the rule). WebKit host `root-x-hidden` (a page with `html { overflow-x: hidden }` and `body { overflow: hidden }`: `<body>` scrolls, a real wheel moves the page, a lock on `<html>` still locks); it fails on the old CSS. New host ops: `wheel` (a real continuous wheel through `scrollWheel`) and `safariAgent` (Safari's user agent, for live sites). The real msu.edu in the host with a wheel: 498 → -502 with the fix, unmoved before.
- **`sleep.test.js`:** the podcast now loops in that test. The tune is 24 s, and with the e2e suite running two files at once the set-up outlasted it; an ended podcast is rightly not playing, so it slept (`slept 4`).

### The window's size and the mouse's position in whole pixels, as Safari's (2026-11-07)

- **Reported:** on youtube.com the sidebar showed only its footer, new videos didn't load on scroll, and a video said the connection was lost until a reload. It works with Margin off. Every YouTube API call (`guide`, `player`, `get_watch`, `log_event`, `get_unseen_count`) answered 400. The YouTube tab was at 115% page zoom (`devicePixelRatio` 2.3).
- **The cause:** at a page zoom the box's insets are fractions in the page's pixels. With them taken off, `innerWidth`/`innerHeight` came out as 810.5 × 681.5, where Safari's are always whole. YouTube sends them in every call as `screenWidthPoints`/`screenHeightPoints`, int32 fields, and its server refuses the whole call: "Invalid value at 'context.client.screen_width_points' (TYPE_INT32), 809.5". This was reproduced in the WebKit host on the real YouTube at 115% with a real window frame. After a reload the first video comes in the page itself, so it played.
- **The fix:** `innerWidth`/`innerHeight` are rounded (content/page/viewport.js), as WebKit rounds its own. The same goes for a real mouse event's `clientX`/`clientY` (and so `x`, `y`, `pageX`, `pageY`) in the box (content/page/coords.js): WebKit gives a mouse event whole pixels and a pointer event fractions, and Margin now does the same. `clientWidth`, `clientHeight` and `offsetHeight` were already whole (WebKit's own values for <body>). `visualViewport` and rectangles are fractions in WebKit too, so they're left alone.
- **Tests:** WebKit host `zoom` now runs with the window's frame told (as Safari: `outerWidth` set, so the box's insets are the layout's in zoomed pixels). At 150% and 115% the window's sizes are whole numbers; a real press at 115% gives the mouse event whole pixels and the pointer event fractions. Both fail on the old code. The real YouTube at 115% in the host: `get_watch` 400 before, 200 after, and the video plays.

### Safari's full-screen toolbar stays Safari's (2026-11-07)

- **Tried and dropped the same day:** hiding Safari's full-screen toolbar under Margin. First Margin covered it while the person reached for the menu bar, with macOS-style window buttons sliding in at the sidebar's top. Feedback: the cover hid the top of the page. Then Margin parked the toolbar's window in a private Space. With Safari's own sidebar open in that window (under Margin's), Safari leaves that column of its toolbar empty: the tabs start about 270 pt in, and Margin's sidebar shows through the glass on the left. Closing Safari's sidebar (View › Hide Sidebar) gives the tabs the whole width.

### Safari's own sidebar kept closed under Margin (2026-11-07)

- **Reported:** "when i reach my cursor on the left edge, it still opens. can we not have it open please." With Keep open on it opened unseen under Margin's docked sidebar; with Keep open off it showed, and it took part of the window, shrinking the page.
- **How the reveal works** (read from AppKit, 2026-11-07: `NSSplitViewController(RevealOnEdgeHover)`). It's AppKit's, for a collapsed sidebar of a full-screen window. It triggers on a mouse-moved event within 4 pt inside the window's leading edge (`NSSplitViewItemFullscreenEdgeInWindowPadding`, default 4; outside the window `…OffWindowPadding`, default 0), after the pointer rests there 0.5 s (`…FullscreenEdgeRevealDelay`). It's heard by local *and global* event monitors, which is why the invisible edge guard over the edge never stopped it. There's also a per-app setting, `NSSplitViewItemRevealsInFullscreen`. Margin doesn't write it: it would outlive Margin (uninstall, the extension off) and would apply to every profile.
- **Three parts, all Margin.app's, only where Margin's layout is drawn over the Safari window in front:**
  - **The edge stop** (`EdgeStop.swift`). While the front window is a full-screen Safari window with Margin's layout, an event tap (Accessibility) moves any mouse-moved event that would land within 5 pt of the window's left edge to 5 pt, and the pointer with it: thrown left, it stops there as at an edge.
    - Margin's own reveal zone (24 pt in full screen) still works.
    - There's no stop where a display lies beside the window's left edge (the pointer crosses there, and crossing never rests).
    - The tap runs on its own thread and is off whenever there's no fence. Nothing is stored; it's gone when Margin quits.
  - **⇧⌘L**, Safari's own sidebar key, is Margin's sidebar key with Safari (`ShortcutSet.bindings(from:safari:)`), as ⌘T is always the palette, unless another Margin command has it in Settings.
  - **Opened anyway** (View › Show Sidebar, the sidebar button in Safari's toolbar): when a part appears on the left of the front window, Margin reads Safari's View menu item (identifier `ShowSidebar`, in any language) by Accessibility.
    - If its title differs from the one learned while nothing showed on the left ("Show Sidebar" against "Hide Sidebar"), it's Safari's sidebar. Margin presses the item once (the menu never opens), and the overlay keeps the whole window meanwhile, covering it.
    - If the title is unchanged, it's something else (a Web Inspector docked on the left): left alone and carved out as before.
    - It's pressed at most once per appearance.
- **The pause after each warp** (reported: "at the very left edge … when i try to move up, it moves up very slowly or doesn't at all"). macOS ignores pointer movement for 0.25 s after a warp by default, and pushed against the stop every move warped. `CGAssociateMouseAndMouseCursorPosition(true)` after the warp didn't lift it. The deprecated `CGSetLocalEventsSuppressionInterval(0)` did (b23d2eb), but nothing deprecated was wanted. Now there's no warp: the pointer is put at the stop by a posted mouse-moved event from Margin's own `CGEventSource` with `localEventsSuppressionInterval = 0` (current API). The posted event lands at the stop, so it passes back through the tap untouched; the event being moved keeps its deltas.
- **Found by the tests:** the cover first passed an infinite docked width, which the left-part log line turned into an integer, trapping. Now it's the window's width.
- **Tests.**
  - `tests.swift`: ⇧⌘L for Safari only, never taking another command's key; the fence (alone, a display beside it, a display left but elsewhere); the clamp; the title rule.
  - `e2e.swift`, with a stand-in for Safari's menu item: the closed title is learned; the fence is set for the full-screen front window; ⇧⌘L is held; the sidebar opens, is closed once and covered meanwhile, never pressed again, then gone; a part on the left with the title unchanged is not pressed and is carved out; the held-key counts are now 7.
  - Real Safari: pending, including whether the menu bar's "View" title flashes on the press.

### A page's own full screen: Margin's layout out of the way (2026-11-07)

- **Reported:** a video's full screen (YouTube's button) inside a full-screen Safari window "doesn't really do fullscreen but leave space on the left … our sidebar's space". The page's box already stepped aside for `:fullscreen` (`box.boxed`, `page-box.js`), but Margin.app never heard of it, so its layer, the sidebar included, stayed over the window.
- **Now:**
  - **The page.** Its top frame tells its copy when it goes into full screen and back (`content/core.js tellFullscreen`). That covers `fullscreenchange`, which includes a video player in a frame, and Safari's own video full screen (`webkitpresentationmodechanged`, `webkitbegin/endfullscreen` on a `<video>`, heard on the capture phase since they don't bubble).
  - **The copy.** It puts `pageFullscreen: true` on the window's entry while that tab is the window's tab in front (`background/link.js pageFullscreen`, `handlers.js`).
  - **The app.** It conceals the overlay over that window (out of sight, the pointer passing through) and skips the rest of its show. It lets go of Margin's keys (⌘T and the rest are the page's then) and the edge stop. Out of full screen, the usual show brings it back.
- **Tests:** `link.test.js` (the tab in front's word on the window's entry, a tab behind's not, gone on the way out); `e2e.swift` (concealed with the pointer passing through, the keys let go and no edge stop, then all back).
- **Still a strip** (a screenshot from real Safari: the video 1244 pt wide at x 260–1504, the box's place, the page's black around it). YouTube's watch page makes `<html>` itself full screen (`ZF(window.document.documentElement)` in its player, `externalFullscreen`). The browser's own full-screen rules, `!important` and so beating the box's, skip the root (`:not(:root):fullscreen`), so the box's `html` rule (its translate and its `100vw` less the insets) stayed. Now `html:fullscreen` makes the box the whole window (no translate, `100vw` × `100vh` in the page's zoomed pixels, the shift variables 0). It's more specific than the box's `html` rule, both `!important`. `<body>` stays the scroller, as Margin's world says. A `<body>` or another element in full screen was already the browser's. Test: `page-css.test.js`. The WebKit host can't go into full screen without taking the real screen, so it isn't tested there.

### Tab keys highlighted at the press; a swipe's space switch asked for as it settles (2026-11-08)

- **Reported:** "the tab switches are not instantaneous sometimes … through cmd option up/down real quick … at least highlight instantaneously", and with a gesture "it takes a while for me to see that space is switching".
- **Where the time went** (the real logs, 2026-11-07 23:59).
  - **The tab keys.** The app sent each press to the copy (`navigate`), which worked out the target, told the overlay to highlight it and asked Safari. Safari's activation came 10–30 ms after the ask. But the copy's background was often still on the switch before ("stored +455 ms", "delta out +530 ms"), or waking, so a quick next press, and its highlight, waited behind it.
  - **A swipe over the sidebar** asked for its space only after its 0.22 s slide-in, which itself starts once the gesture is seen to end (about 0.16 s). Another profile's "switching" cover then came about 60 ms after that.
- **Now:**
  - **Tab keys.** The app hands next/previous-tab to the overlay's page when it's drawn (`Shell.run`; before that, to the copy as before). The page picks the target with the copy's own rule (`shared/switching.js pickNavTab` with `shared/view.js cycleTab`). Each press goes on from the last one's target for `NAV_CHAIN_MS`, else from the tab in front. The page highlights it at once and asks the copy for exactly that tab with its own switch id (`ov-N`). The copy takes that pick as the press's while it's a tab of that window, with the id, both at the press and when it works a target out later (`navigation.js navigate` `given`, `takeGiven`), else works it out as before. Its queue, latest-wins and key-run log are unchanged. The copy's `switching` for those ids is ignored by the page, so it's never moved back by a late one.
  - **Swipe.** Another profile's space is switched to as the swipe settles, so its cover comes at once. One of this profile's has its tab asked of the copy as it settles (`setSpace`), so Safari brings it while the slide comes in, and the space left is held shown till the slide lands (`runtime.holdSpace`), so nothing jumps; the space is then drawn as before. The second `setSpace` at the slide's end finds the tab in front and does nothing more.
- **Not changed:** how fast Safari shows the tab still depends on the copy's background, but now nothing on screen waits for it. The space keys (⌘⌥←/→) still go through the copy.
- **Tests.**
  - `switching-pick.test.js`: order and wrapping, the chain and its end, a closed target, nothing known.
  - `spaces-switch.test.js`: the overlay's pick taken with its id; one not in the window worked out.
  - `e2e.swift`: the key's request carries the page's target and `ov-` id. The highlight itself can't be seen there: an off-screen page is hidden, and a hidden page draws no switch.
  - Theme `behaviors` swipe: `setSpace` asked as it settles, the old space still drawn, the new one as the slide lands.

### After an update: Margin turned off in two profiles; the highlight's echo window (2026-11-08)

- **Reported** after the switching build was installed:
  - switching to another profile's space opened a new window of it, with "Switching to …" left in the window in use;
  - quitting Safari left the hidden windows, which came back as small windows;
  - fast tab keys over loading tabs made the highlight go back to a passed tab and forward again.
- **What happened at the install** (00:38 local time, 05:38 UTC; the real log and Safari's `Extensions.plist` per profile, read only).
  - Margin.app was replaced on disk and quit for the new build, and Safari reloaded Margin's extension in every profile ("1001 going away").
  - In the two profiles where an old **unsigned** Margin build was also switched on, Safari switched the current, team-signed Margin **off** at that moment (`EnabledModificationDate` 05:38). The two profiles with the unsigned one off kept it on. So those profiles' copies never ran again: each switch to them asked Safari for a new window, waited 10 s for a copy that couldn't start, and failed.
  - Their hidden windows couldn't be closed through their copies at Safari's quit either.
  - The old Margin's private Spaces ended with it, so macOS dropped the two parked windows out as normal windows. The new one found them "moved" and left them.
- **Now:**
  - **A turned-off profile.** A switch to a profile whose Margin is turned off (the browser's own settings: `SafariAX.marginEnabled`, read only; `SwitchWorld.marginOff`) fails at once, no window opened and no wait, saying how to turn it on, in both the plain switch and the handoff. The failure notice now says so whether or not a window was opened.
  - **The highlight.** `PASSED_MS` went from 300 ms to 1 s. Safari's answer comes as it activates the newest target, but the state with it in front reached the overlay up to half a second later (the copy busy with the writes before), so a passed tab still in front then is the state lagging. Before, the highlight went back to it and forward again. The chain log showed "ended back on a tab it had passed … went back 1 time" before the switching change too.
- **To do by hand:** turn the old unsigned Margin off, and the current one on, in those two profiles (Safari › Settings › Extensions, each profile chosen at the top).
- **Not done:** windows parked when Margin updates mid-session still come back as normal windows.
- **Tests.**
  - `profiles-tests.swift` and `handoff-tests.swift`: Margin off in the target's profile fails at once with no window asked for, and A stays in front.
  - `switching.test.js`: the newest target answered while the state lags 0.6 s on passed tabs, and the highlight never goes back. It fails at 300 ms.
- **A held key** (reported: "when i stop holding it, it still keeps moving"). Its repeats came faster than a highlight is drawn, so they queued in the overlay's page and went on after the key was let go. Now the page adds up the presses that arrive and takes them once a frame (`overlay.js navTab`/`flushNav`, with a 50 ms timer when no frames come), giving one highlight and one `navigate` for where they end, so none wait.

### The page box's rules and the patterns it handles (2026-11-08)

- **Asked:** the box's edge cases should live in one proper structure, so a fix means adding a scenario or updating one. Then: they aren't site-specific, so not "edge cases": they're named **patterns** (what pages commonly do), each fixed at the root for every page that does it, never for one site.
- **Now:** `tests/box/`.
  - `rules.js`: what the box promises, as nine rules. Two self-contained functions: `measure()` in a page, `judge(boxed, plain, setup)`.
  - The reference is the same page in a plain window the box's size: an iframe that size, in the same browser. That means one engine version on both sides, so the WebKit host isn't compared with Playwright's WebKit.
  - `patterns/*.html`: one small page per pattern, named after the pattern, its header saying what pages do (`pattern:`), where it was first seen (`from:`), what handles it, and anything it's let off (`allow:` with a `note:`). Pages write what they observe into `<output>`s, which are compared too.
  - Run in Chromium by `tests/e2e/box-patterns.test.js`, and in the WebKit host by the generated `box-patterns` scenario (the rules pasted into the check).
  - `README.md`: the module map, the rules and the table of patterns. The rules and table are generated by `readme.mjs`, and `tests/box-patterns.test.js` fails when they drift.
  - The existing box tests stay where they were (they test the box over time and with the rest of Margin). The README lists them.
- **Two bugs fit-check found, fixed with their patterns first (each failing before):**
  - `html-class-width` (islonline.net): Bootstrap's `.w-100 { width: 100% !important }` on `<html>` beat the box's `html { … !important }`, so the box went back to the window's width. The box's `<html>` rule is now `BOX_ROOT` (`html:not(#m#m#m#m#m)`), as are the full-screen rule (one step heavier) and the first paint's. It failed in Chromium and the WebKit host before.
  - `offcanvas-into-view` (go.dev): with a box, what's fixed is placed in `<html>`, so a drawer moved off the box's edge with a transform runs past the window. `scrollIntoView` of a link in it scrolled the window itself, with every shim still saying 0. `content/page/viewport.js` now puts the window's own scroll back to 0 on a trusted scroll of the document, not under a pinch. It failed in Chromium only: WebKit didn't scroll the window for it.
- **Known and let off:** `scroll-lock`. While a lock (`body { position: fixed; top: -300px }`) is on, the page is told it's still scrolled 300px (plain: 0), because Margin keeps `<body>` the scroller and doesn't let the lock move it. What's drawn is the same.
- **Tests:** `tests/box-patterns.test.js` (unit), `tests/e2e/box-patterns.test.js` (10 patterns, Chromium), the WebKit host's `box-patterns` (10), `page-css` and `build` (the weighted selectors).

### The page box split by what each part does (2026-11-08)

- **Asked:** the box's code should be easier to read and maintain.
- **Now:** `content/page/box.js` was one 810-line function with about 60 functions sharing its variables. It's now the box itself (placing and moving it, on and off, the bridge) and five parts it starts:
  - `box-own-sheets.js`: Margin's sheets, kept adopted.
  - `box-locks.js`: `<body>`'s scrolling, the page's scroll locks, the background.
  - `box-body.js`: one read of what the page says about `<body>`, and applying it.
  - `box-chain.js`: the first children whose top margins count.
  - `box-watch.js`: when to read again.
  - `shared/body-fit.js`: the arithmetic, pure and tested in node.
- **How the parts share:** what more than one part reads or writes (`html`, `sized`, `lastSaid`, `lastPage`, `pageNew`, `plainPage`, `refused`) is on one `ctx`, with each part's functions the others call. Everything else stays inside its part. The browser's own functions are still taken before `viewport.js` speaks for the box, and everything is set up in the same order as before.
- **Not changed:** what any of it does. The code moved as it was, its comments with it. The box's functions are plain calls through `ctx`, so nothing outside the box saw a difference.
- **Tests:** `tests/body-fit.test.js` (new: pixels, collapsing, the width equation for plain, centred, max-width and padding, right to left, zoomed). `box-patterns` in both engines, `tests/e2e/page-box.test.js`, and the WebKit host's box scenarios (`box`, `hidden-box`, `toggle`, `undrawn`, `csp`, `lock`, `late-body`, `read-limits`, `late-reads`, `read-shape`, `body-size`, `body-background`, `in-view`, `answers`, `keys`, `history`, `top-layer`, `linked-sheet`, `first-paint`, `first-paint-off`) pass as they did. Then the full gate.

### Keys after a click in Margin's UI go to the browser (2026-11-08)

- **Reported:** ⌘R reloads from the page, but after a click in the sidebar it beeps, as if the shortcut weren't there.
- **Why:** Margin's overlay is a non-activating panel, never key unless a field of Margin's has the focus. A click in such a panel moves the keyboard to Margin.app without making it the active app. Safari stays in front, but the keys come to Margin.app, which has no key window for them: the system's beep. Nothing logged "took the keyboard", because the overlay never did.
- **Now:**
  - `OverlayController.pressEnded`: when a press in the overlay (or its edge panel) ends, after `pressSettle` (80 ms, so a field the press focused can say `focus` first), the keyboard goes back to the browser as `handBack` gives it (`returnKeyboard`: yield and activate). Not if the overlay has the keyboard or its page asked for it (`handsKeyboardBack`).
  - `Shell.startKeyRelay`, a safety net: a key that reaches Margin.app with none of Margin's windows key, while a linked browser is in front, is posted on to that browser (press and release, as it would have had them) and the keyboard returned (`relayTarget`). Margin already posts keys to the browser (⌘Q, `postQuitKeys`). Which key isn't logged, only a count.
  - Neither runs in a harness.
- **Tests:** `tools/app-tests/tests.swift` checks `handsKeyboardBack` and `relayTarget`. The app tests can't press a real panel (nothing is shown or made key there), so the press itself is to be checked in Safari.

### A <body> placed by its own offset sits where the page puts it (2026-11-08)

- **Found by fit-check (xkcd.com):** `body { position: absolute; left: 50%; width: 780px; margin-left: -390px }`. In the box the column started 390px left of the box, the comic cut off.
- **Why:** the box's `<body>` rule had `inset: auto !important`, so that a scroll lock's `top: -Ypx` couldn't move the scroller. It also took away the page's `left: 50%`, keeping only the width and the negative margin, which the box gave back as `margin-left: -390px`.
- **Now:**
  - Only `top` and `bottom` are held by the box's `<body>` rule (scroll locks).
  - The page's sideways offset is read with its size and margins (`readSaid` `offset`: `left`'s used value, with the fit sheet off, `right` counted in). It's given back with the margins (`shared/body-fit.js resolve`, `readLaidOut`): what it adds on the left comes off the right.
  - The fit sheet holds `left` and `right` at `auto`, as it holds the width.
- **Pattern:** `tests/box/patterns/body-centred-by-offset.html`, failing in Chromium and the WebKit host before.
- **Tests:** `body-fit` (xkcd's numbers: its column at 196 in 1172), `page-css` (top and bottom held, not left and right; the fit sheet's left and right). The WebKit host's `lock` and the other box scenarios pass as before.

### The box's CSS variables are --margin-box-* (2026-11-08)

The box put its own `--margin-left: 260px` and `--margin-top: 8px` on `<html>`, so every container that set none of its own inherited them: whole sections 260px to the right and 8px down. Any page or framework using such a name met the box's values.

They're set in `shared/page-box.js`, `shared/page-css.js` and `background/registered.js`, with the themes' first-paint files, the tests, the WebKit host and `app/PROTOCOL.md` to match. A page's own `--margin-*` is its own again.
- **Pattern:** `tests/box/patterns/page-css-variables.html`, failing in Chromium and the WebKit host before.

### Another origin's style sheet copied whole, its imports in it (2026-11-08)

- **Found by fit-check (anu.edu.au):** its CDN sheet imports Bootstrap's grid as `@import"../../libs/bootstrap/css/bootstrap-grid.min.css"` (minified, no space). Margin's readable copy of an unreadable sheet (`content/page-link.js`) made `url()` and `@import "…"` absolute, but its pattern wanted a space after `@import`. The address stayed relative, resolved against the page and wasn't found, and the grid was lost: the site's container 1172px wide where it makes it 960.
- **Also:** an import of another origin's in the copy is itself unreadable, so its media queries stayed the window's, even with the address right.
- **Now:**
  - `shared/sheet-copy.js`: `absolute` takes `@import` with a space or not.
  - `inlineImports` puts what a copy imports into it, fetched the same way (the background's `fetchStyle`): in place, inside `@media …` for a media list, their own imports in them, 3 levels and 20 imports at most, `@charset` dropped.
  - If any import can't go in (not fetched, in a layer, under `supports()`), none does and they stay absolute `@import`s, since an import after a rule would be dropped.
  - `page-link.js` uses both, and checks again after the inlining that the link is still what it copied.
- **Patterns:** `cross-origin-import.html` (a second origin, `{{other}}` in a pattern's page: `box-cdn.test` in the e2e harness, `localhost` in the WebKit host; failing in both before). `async-stylesheet.html` (a sheet loaded media print, switched as it loads: passing before too, kept as a guard, and the first guess at springer.com's overflow, which turned out to be its own `overflow: hidden` on `<body>`). `serve.js` serves a pattern's files (`patterns/assets/`).
- **Tests:** `tests/sheet-copy.test.js`.

### The box's IntersectionObserver lists its methods, as the browser's does (2026-11-08)

- **Found by fit-check (gog.com):** 293 errors through Margin, `this.viewportEnterObserver.observe is not a function`. gog is an Angular app, and zone.js replaces `IntersectionObserver` with a wrapper whose prototype gets a method for each function it finds listing a sample instance with `for…in`. The box's stand-in (`content/page/in-view.js`) had `observe`, `unobserve`, `disconnect` and `takeRecords` as own properties that weren't enumerable, which hid the browser's (enumerable, on its prototype) from `for…in`. The wrapper had no `observe`, and nothing Angular watched came into view.
- **Now:** the stand-in's methods and getters are enumerable. gog's Margin-only errors went from 264 to 1.
- **Pattern:** `tests/box/patterns/observer-wrapped.html` (zone.js's patchClass, in the page), failing before.
- **Also:**
  - A pattern's page can arrive in parts (`<!--pause:N-->`, `serve.js partsOf`; both servers send them apart).
  - `early-head-script.html` checks that a script early in `<head>` sees the box.
  - The header check now takes the header's own end, so a comment quoted inside a header (which ends it early) fails.
- **Not found yet:**
  - simpli.fi: React's hydration errors (#418), through Margin only, in Chromium and the WebKit host. The markup before hydration is the same, and no one shim switched off makes them go. A guess at the page script's start (looking again for each node in `<head>`) made no difference and was taken back.
  - cxense.com: blank, because Framer's script writes `translateY(-1000px)` on its fixed hero through Margin and not plain.
  - stuff.co.nz: the site's own "something went wrong".
  - 1und1.de: didn't load through Margin.

### What the box costs, measured (2026-11-08)

- **Asked:** while fixing these, don't make Margin slower.
- **Now:**
  - `npm run bench:box` (`tests/box/bench.mjs`): a heavy page (`serve.js benchPage`: 20,000 rules, a fifth with viewport units and a tenth in media queries, 3,000 elements) and a smaller one (2,000 and 500), 7 loads each, through Margin in Chromium and plain, the medians of the page's load and from load to its second frame. The box's cost is what it adds, compared with `bench-baseline.json`; it fails past a quarter more and 30 ms.
  - Baseline from `main` before the day's fixes (d4240ec): the box adds 123 ms to the heavy page's load and 33 to the small one's, nothing after load.
  - With the fixes: 122 and 25.
  - fit-check's summary has a Speed line: how much slower pages load through Margin than plain, the median and the slowest tenth, every night. Round 1: 12 ms faster at the median, 242 ms slower at the slowest tenth, 145 of 2,651 sites over half a second slower.
  - The imports in a copied sheet are fetched all at once (`inlineImports`), so the copy waits for the slowest, not their sum.

### The document's scroller is <html> again, and scroll timelines run on the box's (2026-11-08)

- **Found by fit-check (cxense.com, blank):** Framer's motion takes its container from `document.scrollingElement` and the window's height from that element's `clientHeight`. The box answered `scrollingElement` with `<body>`, the element that really scrolls, but `<body>`'s `clientHeight` is the page's height, as in a window (7933, not 884). Framer worked out that the page had scrolled through, and put its fixed hero at its end, 1000px up.
- **Now:**
  - `document.scrollingElement` is what a window's is: `<html>` (`<body>` in quirks mode). `<html>`'s scrolling already speaks for `<body>` (`viewport.js`: scrollTop, scrollHeight, clientHeight, scrollTo…), so everything read through it is the window's, and `<body>`'s own `clientHeight` stays the page's.
  - `content/page/timelines.js`: a `ScrollTimeline` on `<html>`, or with no source, is made on the box's scroller. In the box `<html>` doesn't scroll, and a timeline on it is inactive (`currentTime` null), which libraries read as the end. It's still the browser's own `ScrollTimeline`.
  - Margin's own scripts in the isolated world see the browser's `scrollingElement`, as before.
- **Rules:** `body-scrolls` became `same-scroller`: `document.scrollingElement` and its height are what they are in a plain window. The overflow measure looks at `<body>`'s overflow where the box makes `<html>` clip. The WebKit host's `boxed()` and two checks now expect `<html>`.
- **Patterns:** `scrolling-element.html`, `scroll-timeline.html` (failing before; cxense renders now).
- **Speed:** `bench:box` within the noise (the box's cost 131 and 35 ms; baseline 123 and 33, an earlier run 122).


## TypeScript (2026-11-09)

- **Asked:** the code in TypeScript, all of it, with the faster native compiler, no feature lost and nothing slower.
- **The compiler:** TypeScript 7 (Microsoft's native port, written in Go) was already the type checker (`typescript@7.0.2`, about 0.6 s for the whole check). The Rust ports (Oxc's `tsrs` 0.23, `tsc-rs` 0.8) are pre-1.0 and track a TypeScript beta; the choice was to stay on TypeScript 7.
- **What changed:**
  - Every `.js` became `.ts` (`.mjs` → `.mts`), with every JSDoc type moved into TypeScript syntax where it was: parameters, return types, generics, variables, casts (`(x as T)`), typedefs (`export type` / `interface`), `@import` (`import type`). A one-off converter did it from TypeScript 7's own parse of the JSDoc (its API), so each type is the one the checker read; the comments keep their words.
  - Imports are spelled `.ts`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly` are on: Node runs the tests and scripts from the `.ts` files as they are (its type stripping, Node 26), and esbuild bundles them for the browsers.
  - The checks are as strict as before (`strict` off), and also cover Margin.app's overlay page now. Where JavaScript let things pass that TypeScript doesn't, the types say what JavaScript assumed: class fields `declare`d with the types the checker had inferred for them; objects given properties later typed with those properties; trailing parameters that callers leave out marked optional (in JavaScript every parameter is); and `types/js-defaults.d.ts` keeps JavaScript's `any` for a generic call with nothing to infer from (`Object.values`/`entries`, `Array.from`, a `Map` or `Set` of an untyped value) where TypeScript would say `unknown`.
  - The build bundles from the `.ts` sources and no longer ships them in `dist/` (no page loaded them: every context is a bundle). The one file a browser loads as it is, `content/page/fullscreen-only.js` (Chrome's registration), is written from its `.ts`.
  - Still JavaScript: the files a browser loads raw or that are pasted into a bundle (`tools/handoff-lab/ext/`, `tools/webkit-host/hook.js`, `tools/boards/dc-shim.js`).
  - The tests and tools are TypeScript too, run as they are; like before, they aren't type-checked (that's thousands of errors in their fakes: a later step).
- **Nothing slower, nothing changed at run time:** every bundle Safari, Chrome and Margin.app load was compared byte for byte with the build from `main` before the change. The background, content, new-tab, stand-in and overlay bundles are identical; the page's bundle differs in file names inside CSS comments and one arrow function in parentheses; `arcadia.js` in a comment.
- **File names before this date** in this log are the `.js` ones they were then.
