## Chrome and Edge link to Margin.app on the Mac (2026-11-09)

- **Asked:** Chrome and Edge working with Margin.app as Safari does. Until now only Safari linked (PLAN.md Phase 5 was never built).
- **How:** the same link as Safari's, found another way (app/PROTOCOL.md "Transport (Chrome and Edge, on the Mac)"). Chrome and Edge can't hear `SFSafariApplication.dispatchMessage`, so a relay helper inside Margin.app (`Contents/Helpers/margin-relay`, `app/relay/main.swift`), started by the browser through native messaging, does what Safari's extension handler does: it passes the copy's messages to Margin.app over a Unix socket only this user can open (`RelayLink.swift`), and Margin.app's answers back, the `link` and `appUp` dispatched into the copy's lasting port as Safari's are. The copy then opens the same WebSocket as Safari's, from Chrome's service worker (WebKit's worker hang is Safari's alone: the socket guard stays Safari's). Phase 0's spike carried every message over the native port instead; reusing the WebSocket keeps one link, already tested, for every browser.
- **Trust:** the relay socket is mode 0600, and Margin.app lets in only this user's processes, and in a signed build only Margin's relay signed by the same team (`identifier "io.tirth.margin.relay"`, the team from the app's own signature). The host files name only Margin's extension (`allowed_origins`). The token and key work as for Safari.
- **The Chrome build** has a fixed `key` (platform/chrome/manifest.json), so its ID is `njeebbcmlenfopaecfbphgcfihbdmkec` everywhere, the one the host files name (tests/build.test.ts checks the two agree). Its private key is outside the repo (`~/.margin/chrome-extension-key.pem`, the development Mac): it's needed to keep that ID on the Chrome Web Store. A Chrome build loaded before had another ID: it comes back as a new extension.
- **Built:** Chrome's and Edge's host files written at each launch (`ChromiumHosts.swift`: Chrome and its Beta, Dev and Canary, Edge and its Beta, Dev and Canary, where the browser's folder exists); the relay built universal and signed into the app by `scripts/safari.sh`, the app signed again around it; `hello` saying `chrome` or `edge` (Edge's user agent has `Edg/`) and the browser's process (the relay's parent); pages' visibility reports on wherever the app links (the window matcher uses them).
- **Safari's only, on purpose:** the profile handoff and parking (their sweep, checks and recovery read Safari's windows): Chrome's and Edge's profiles switch the close-based way, and the notice for a profile not open says to open one of its windows from the browser's profile menu (Margin can't ask Chrome for one). Also Safari's: iCloud Tabs, Accessibility's exact window binding, the startup covers, the edge stop, keeping Safari's sidebar closed.
- **Tests:** the link in Chrome's build (`tests/link-chromium.test.ts`); the real relay with the app's real listener and SocketLink (`tools/app-tests/relay-tests.swift`); Chrome for Testing, headless, loading the real Chrome build and starting the real relay through native messaging, linking to a stand-in app (`tests/e2e/chromium-relay.test.ts`). Safari's bundles differ only by the switches above, each the same as before for Safari (read in the diffs).
- **Next (Phase 5's rest):** checks by hand in real Chrome and Edge (TESTING.md "Chrome and Edge on the Mac"); their profiles' own names (`Local State`); the iCloud Tabs folder's counterpart from `sessions.getDevices()`; Chrome's full-screen toolbar windows, which the matcher hasn't been shown yet.

## Margin for Windows planned: a Rust shell, macOS first still (2026-11-09)

Decided ("let's do it in rust then … write app for windows for now"). It supersedes "Margin 2 ships for macOS
only" (2026-11-04) for Windows; Linux stays later and undecided (`native/BRIEF.md`). The macOS app, its Swift shell and
the Safari build are untouched by this work, which lives on `feat/windows-shell` in its own worktree.

- **Where the code is.** `native/` is a Cargo workspace: `margin-core`, OS-neutral (the link's session and messages,
  chunks, the state mirror, the window binder and map, pass-through, the overlay planner, keys, the data set, store,
  sync, browser profiles, imported themes, spaces across profiles, the close-based profile switch), each module naming
  the Swift file it ports and tested on the Mac with the Swift's own tests and vectors (`tests/fixtures/data-merge`,
  `tests/fixtures/traces`); and `margin-windows`, the binary `margin.exe`. Nothing has run on Windows: every behaviour
  only Windows can confirm is a line in `native/UNVERIFIED.md`, with how to check it.
- **No WebSocket on Windows.** Only Chrome and Edge exist there, and they link through native messaging: `margin.exe`,
  started by the browser as its host, relays the port to the running app over a named pipe for this user only
  (`\\.\pipe\Margin-<SID>`, a DACL for the user, remote clients refused, first instance only, each end checking the
  other is the same `margin.exe`). The pipe carries native messaging's own framing (4-byte little-endian length, UTF-8
  JSON) and the link's messages unchanged. So `margin-core` ports the link's session rules (welcome, hello in 5 s,
  owner, replaced, tick/tock, 40 s, requests in 15 s, the 1 MB cap), not the RFC 6455 framing, the token, the Origin
  check or Safari's dispatch. The welcome's `key` is optional: the pipe's security stands in for it.
- **The extension's half of the Chromium link** comes from the macOS work (the relay helper on the Mac, PLAN.md
  "Spike 3"), not built a second time here. Until it lands: the Chrome manifest has no `nativeMessaging` permission,
  no extension id is fixed (`install.rs EXTENSION_IDS` is empty, `MARGIN_EXTENSION_IDS` for unpacked builds), and the
  relay's own frames (`relayHello`, `relayWelcome`, `relayDown`, `relayUp`) are this branch's, to align with the Mac's.
  The relay's facts win over the copy's: a link's browser (Edge or Chrome) and pid come from the relay's parent process.
- **The overlay page is shared.** Its one change: `extension/ui/overlay-bridge.ts` picks WebKit's handler (the Mac, as
  before) or WebView2's (`chrome.webview.postMessage` with a `rid`, answered `{ reply: rid, ok, value | error }`; the
  app answers every message). The Safari and Chrome bundles are byte-identical to main's; `dist/app/overlay.js` differs
  only by the bridge.
- **Overlays on Windows:** a no-activate tool popup per browser window, not owned by it (a cross-process owner ties
  the two UI threads' input together), kept just above it in z-order and restacked on foreground changes; WebView2 by
  composition (transparent); pointer pass-through by toggling `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT` from the pointer's place, as
  `PointerWatch` does; the overlay files served by the app with the Mac's Content Security Policy, every other request
  refused. Taking the keyboard (the palette) makes the overlay the foreground window: Windows has no non-activating
  key panel.
- **Windowed windows too on Windows** (2026-11-09, as most people there don't use F11): Margin draws over
  every linked Chrome or Edge window, over the whole window in full screen and over the page area only otherwise,
  under the tabs and toolbar (`planner::windowed_frame`; the shell's `windowed_too`, off on the Mac). Its layout is
  measured from where the copy takes its page to be, so `boxFromLayout` puts the page's box at the slot without
  knowing about Windows' invisible borders.
- **A copy's process is trusted, as on the Mac** (2026-11-09): a Chrome or Edge copy's `hello.pid` is never
  checked against the connectors before linking, but both apps log a warning at link up when no connector's hello
  has named that process since the app started (`Shell.unheardPid` in Swift, `warn_unheard_pid` in margin-core).
- **Keys on Windows are provisional, to pick later:** next/previous tab Ctrl+Alt+↓/↑, space Ctrl+Alt+→/←, palette
  Ctrl+T, sidebar Alt+S, new window Ctrl+N. Ctrl+Alt is AltGr on many European layouts, and some graphics drivers take
  Ctrl+Alt+arrows. Only the combinations the copy writes for the Mac (`Meta+KeyT`, the built-in navigation keys,
  `Meta+KeyN`) are swapped for these; a key recorded in Settings is kept as written (Chrome on Windows reports the
  Windows key as `Meta`).
- **What doesn't carry over** (each said in its module): Spaces and the own-Space checks, the full-screen handoff with
  parking and the freeze (SkyLight), Safari's Accessibility, files, profile names and sidebar, iCloud Tabs (`cloudTabs`
  is null; `sessions.getDevices()` could stand in later), covers, EdgeStop. Profile names for Chromium can come from
  `Local State` later (`browserId`/`browserName` are kept for it).
- **Bugs the ports found in the Swift** (not fixed on the Mac by this branch): two wrong bindings in
  `WindowMatcher.swift` past the gate's seed ranges (the space-switch run's seed 1686, the pages run's seed 1084: the
  Swift tests reproduce them); `DataStore.save` can write over a later format's files when a save is a profile's first
  touch; a failed save in `DataSync.carry` leaves that link held for good; `ProfileSwitch.undo` leaves a window it made
  when the switch started from none; `Combo.parse` drops F13 and up; `spaceContent`'s caps take an arbitrary subset.
  The Rust ports avoid the data ones and keep the binder's for comparison.
- **Update (2026-11-09): Windows links as the Mac does** (the restructure), superseding "No WebSocket on Windows"
  above and the relay's facts winning. Each copy opens its own WebSocket to 127.0.0.1 (welcome with the key, hello,
  every message the same): margin-core ports LinkSocket.swift and ExtensionLink.swift's `SocketLink` sans IO
  (`websocket.rs`, `socket.rs`), margin.exe holds the TCP sockets (`tcp.rs`). The named pipe is for finding the app
  only: Margin's connector (`margin-connector.exe`, beside `margin.exe`) is the browsers' host on every OS, and
  margin-core's `relay.rs` answers it as RelayLink.swift does. margin.exe's relay mode, its pipe framing and host
  registration are gone; the welcome's key is always there; the hello's browser and pid are trusted as on the Mac.
  The Chromium build's `linksApp` is the Mac and Windows. docs/windows/BRIEF.md has why.

## The repo's layout: extension, app, docs (2026-11-09)

The layout (approved page: the folder map), on branch `refactor/repo-layout`. **Paths in the entries above,
from before 2026-11-09, are the old ones** (`platform/`, `app/shell/`, `app/overlay/`, `app/relay/`, `app/safari/`,
`native/`, `tools/app-tests/*-tests.swift`, `dist/safari/`, `dist/chrome/`); the history keeps them as they were.

- **The folders.** The root is split by program only: `extension/`, `app/`, `docs/`. Each program keeps its own
  per-browser side in its `engines/` (asked the same day: an `engines/` at the root holding `extension/` and `app/`
  again was confusing): `extension/engines/{webkit/safari,chromium}/` (manifest, profile, own modules, tests) and
  `app/engines/{webkit/safari,chromium}/` (Safari's Swift and extension handler; Chromium's host files in Rust). Safari
  is WebKit's only browser, so WebKit's code is Safari's; Chromium's is shared by Chrome, Edge and the rest until one
  of them needs its own `chromium/<browser>/`. The build never copies `extension/engines/` into a `dist/` folder (its
  code is bundled from there), so the builds came out byte-identical to before the move (567 files).
  `app/shared/{core,connector,host}/` is Margin's app on every OS (core and the connector in Rust, host the page drawn
  over each browser window, the old `app/overlay/`), `app/platforms/macos/{shell,private,startup}/` the Mac's Swift,
  `app/platforms/windows/` the Windows shell (Rust, merged from `feat/windows-shell`). `docs/` holds the protocol, the handoff,
  the data, the private APIs and the Windows notes. Only the `engines/` folders may ask which engine or browser this
  is; shared code asks what the browser can do.
- **`app/platforms/` and `capabilities`** (asked the same day). Each OS's own code is in `app/platforms/{macos,windows,
  linux}/` (Linux a README until it starts), so `app/` reads as `shared/`, `engines/` (per browser) and `platforms/`
  (per OS). `shared/platform.ts` became `shared/capabilities.ts` (export `capabilities`, type `Capabilities`, each
  engine's `capabilities.ts`, `#engine/capabilities`, the debug global `Margin.capabilities`): it was named after the
  old `platform/` folder of per-browser manifests and never meant the OS. The shared module re-exports its engine's
  object (one binding, so the bundle's name stays `capabilities`; the e2e harness patches that exact text). The UI
  runtime's own `platform` (the host's browser, OS and features, handed to themes) is a different thing and kept.
- **One build per engine, with only its own code.** `dist/webkit/` (Safari) and `dist/chromium/` (Chrome, Edge and the
  other Chromium browsers), plus `dist/app/`. Each engine's capabilities (`capabilities.ts`: what its browser can do, the
  old `PROFILES` of `shared/platform.ts`, which is now `shared/capabilities.ts`) and its own modules (`engine.ts`: Safari's `onboarding.ts` and
  `newtab-hint.ts`, Chromium's `fullscreen.ts`) are in its folder. Shared code reaches them as `#engine` and
  `#engine/capabilities`, mapped in `package.json` `"imports"` by condition: the build passes `margin-webkit` or
  `margin-chromium` to esbuild, so the other engine's modules and profile aren't in its bundles (about 2.3 KB less
  background each; the size gain is small, the point is the structure). Unbuilt (unit tests in Node, `tsc`),
  `default` resolves them to `extension/shared/any-engine*.ts`, which pick by the extension's URL as before. esbuild's
  sync API takes no plugins, hence conditions rather than a resolver. The build now bundles from the sources
  themselves (no stamped copy of `capabilities.ts`). The remaining `platform.name` checks became capabilities
  (`socketInWorker`, `socketGuard`, `pageCommandKeys`, `linksApp`, `browser`). Every build's default shortcuts, by the
  id settings save them under, are one table (`shared/navigation-defaults.ts`), since settings can come from another
  browser's copy. Verified: unit 965, theme 267, security 242, e2e 144 + 2 todo, WebKit host 33, the Swift 2046, and an
  Xcode build whose extension is byte-identical to `dist/webkit/` (bundle id unchanged, so Safari takes it as an update).
- **One Rust workspace at the root** (`Cargo.toml`: `app/shared/core`, `app/shared/connector`, `app/platforms/windows`,
  `app/engines/chromium`), `npm run test:rust` (format, clippy with warnings failing, tests, and both Windows targets
  compile-checked when rustup has them), in the gate and in `test:quick` when a crate changes.
- **The connector, in Rust, for every OS** (`app/shared/connector/`, binary `margin-connector`), replacing the Swift
  relay helper. The same protocol (`docs/PROTOCOL.md`); the socket is now `~/Library/Application Support/Margin/
  connector.sock` and the helper `Contents/Helpers/margin-connector`, signed as `io.tirth.margin.connector` (the app's
  peer check names it). It writes the browsers' host files itself (`--install`, `app/engines/chromium/`, crate
  `margin-chromium`: Chrome, Edge, their channels, Brave, Chromium; macOS, Linux, and on Windows the file plus each
  browser's registry key), so `ChromiumHosts.swift` is gone; Margin.app runs it at launch. The app's version is built
  into it (`MARGIN_APP_VERSION`, from the built app's Info.plist in `scripts/safari.sh`), as the Swift one read it from
  the bundle. Edge is told from Chrome by the parent program's own name only (not a folder above it, which could say
  "edge"). Compile-checked for Windows only; the Windows shell still uses its own frames until it moves to this
  protocol. A Chrome or Edge left open across this update keeps its old relay waiting on the old socket: quit and
  reopen it once (TESTING.md says so).
- **Tests beside what they test.** Each app folder's Swift checks are in its `tests/` (`app/platforms/macos/shell/tests/`,
  `app/platforms/macos/private/tests/`, `app/engines/webkit/safari/tests/`), which `tools/app-tests/run.sh` finds from
  `app/platforms/macos/swift-sources.txt` and the app never compiles (it takes each folder's own `*.swift` only); Safari's own
  unit tests are in `extension/engines/webkit/safari/tests/` (`npm test` runs `engines/**/tests/*.test.ts`,
  `test:quick` follows `#engine` imports). Whole-system tests stay in `tests/` (e2e, theme,
  security) and `tools/` (the app's e2e, the WebKit host).
- **The handoff lab builds again** (`tools/handoff-lab/build.sh` failed on main with 46 errors: the switch's code had
  grown to need `Handoff.swift`, `WindowMatcher.swift`, `Parking.swift` and the data files). It now takes those, leaves
  every `extension Shell` out of its copies (not only `BridgeParker.swift`'s), and `SwitchNotice` moved from
  `ShellProfiles.swift` (a Shell extension) to `ProfileSwitch.swift`, which uses it; the lab's own run record is
  `LabHandoffRun` (the shell has a `HandoffRun`).

## Neo-brutalism is Neubrutalism (2026-11-10)

The chosen name for the theme. Its id, folder and name: `neubrutalism`, `extension/themes/neubrutalism/`,
"Neubrutalism" (its CSS kept its own `nb-` prefix).

- **Saved settings follow it.** `state/model.ts` `OLD_NAMES` maps a saved `neo-brutalism` to `neubrutalism`, as it
  does Arcadia's earlier names, and its saved settings (`settings.themes['neo-brutalism']`) move to the new id when
  there are none under it. Package themes had no carry-over of their settings before (only the themes in
  `themes/index.ts`'s `THEMES` did, Arcadia alone): `normalizeThemes` now does it for every renamed package theme.
- **Safari's registration.** While Neo-brutalism was the theme, its first paint was registered as
  `content/layout/theme-neo-brutalism.css`; Safari loads none of an extension's registrations if one names a missing
  file (2026-10-25), so that path stays in the build, empty (`scripts/build.ts` `LEGACY_FILES`), until no Safari has it.
- **The old id stays reserved.** `ThemeStore.swift` `builtins` and `margin-core` `data::themes::BUILTINS` refuse it for
  an imported theme as they refuse the built-ins' own, since a saved `neo-brutalism` now means Neubrutalism.

## A link that's there at once, and a helper instead of the app at login (2026-11-10)

The request: link instantly when the browser starts and stay linked until it quits; and not the whole app always
running. Measured first (the Mac's log, 24 h): 114 of 743 of the app's `dispatchMessage` hand-offs refused
(`SFErrorDomain 1`, every profile alike), once 19 in a row for 10.5 min (the startup cover's 6 s blank, then no
Margin); the extension's background starting 40 times a day, each time asking from scratch. Design and research:
the scratchpad's `instant-link-design.md` and `link-platform-research.md` (summarised here).

- **The link in the handler's own answer.** Margin.app keeps where its link is in the extension's container
  (`Library/Caches/margin-link`, `ExtensionLink.swift` `LinkNote`: owner-only, replaced whole, removed when the
  listener goes; none under the app's tests). The handler answers a copy's `wantLink` with it when the process
  that wrote it is a running Margin.app: the link reaches that copy alone, in milliseconds, with nothing Safari can
  refuse. No App Group: the container is the one the handler's launch note already shares with the app. The old
  way (the notification, then `dispatchMessage`) stays for a note that isn't there.
- **The cause of the 10 minutes:** a second registered Margin.app. `scripts/safari.sh --no-install` (added the same
  night for the release workflow) skipped the install's unregistering of the build's own copy, and Safari took the
  installed app for another app's. It now unregisters its build; and Margin.app itself, at launch and after three
  refused hand-offs in a row (at most once a minute), unregisters copies of itself left in build folders, the Trash
  or gone from disk (`BundleWatch.strays`; never another install) and registers itself again (`Registration`).
- **No cover for nothing.** With the hand-off refused twice in a row no layout is coming: covers go at once
  (`CoverPlan.Facts.linkStalled`), and none is made, instead of holding 6 s.
- **margin-helper** (`app/platforms/macos/helper/`), the login agent (`SMAppService.agent`,
  `io.tirth.margin.helper.plist`, in Margin.app's `Contents/Library/LaunchAgents`, its program `Contents/Helpers/`):
  it starts Margin.app (`--background`) as a browser opens, about 0.3 s, long before the extension asks (about 3 s
  after Safari opens). 2.5 MB (9 MB resident) where the waiting app was 44 MB. It follows launches by observing
  `NSWorkspace.runningApplications`: the launch notifications reach only a process connected as an app, which
  costs 50 MB. Margin.app now quits a minute after the last browser closes, and the 10-minute idle rule quits
  instead of restarting it to wait. The app's own login item becomes the helper's once, on if it was on (or never
  added), off if it had been turned off. A build without the helper (an Xcode run's) works as before.
  `tools/app-tests/helper-test.sh` tries it off screen with stand-ins for a browser and Margin.app.
- **No page needed:** the extension's background starts by itself as the browser opens (about 3 s after Safari's
  launch, in every session logged), on the Start Page, an empty window or none.
- **Next:** Margin's UI drawn from its own data as a window binds, before the copy links (Safari takes ~3 s to
  start the extension, which no link can beat); the connector answering Chrome's and Edge's ask the same way;
  why Safari's `storage.session` kept no link across a background restart (every one logged said "kept link: no").

## Margin's identifiers are Unibox's: com.unibox.margin (2026-11-10)

Margin belongs to the Unibox organization on GitHub (`uniboxed/margin`), but its identifiers carried a person's name.
Before the first release, while nobody has it installed, they're `com.unibox.margin`: the app, the Safari extension
(`com.unibox.margin.Extension`), margin-helper (`com.unibox.margin.helper`, its plist renamed with it), the connector
(`com.unibox.margin.connector`), the native-messaging host Chrome and Edge ask for (`com.unibox.margin`, its host
files with it), the log's subsystem, the preferences' domain and the notifications. The entries above keep the old
name (`io.tirth.margin`): they're the history.

- **`com.`, not `company.`** (the org's site is unibox.company, which reverses to `company.unibox`, as Arc's
  `company.thebrowser.Browser`): chosen for the familiar form. Bundle ids aren't checked against a domain.
- **No migration in the app.** Its data was never under the id (`~/Library/Application Support/Margin/`, the app
  isn't sandboxed). What is keyed by it, only on the one Mac that ran it, was moved there by hand: the preferences'
  domain, the old login agent and host files. Safari takes the renamed extension for a new one: it's turned on
  again once; the default profile's spaces are `s-default` either way, and named profiles' sets are carried over by
  Safari's own profile ids (`BrowserProfiles.carrySource`) once Margin.app has Full Disk Access again (macOS ties
  its permissions to the id, as it does Accessibility's).
- **Signed by the person still.** The Developer ID certificate names its Individual team's holder; only an Apple
  Organization account (a registered company and a D-U-N-S number) signs as Unibox. v0.1.0 ships with the
  Individual team; a switch later changes the team id, and the permissions are given again once.
- **Not registered with Apple.** A Developer ID app without restricted capabilities needs no registered App ID
  (the team had none, the old id included); the API key's role can't register one. Registering
  `com.unibox.margin` in the developer portal only reserves it.
- **The Chrome extension's id doesn't change:** it comes from its key (`njeebbcmlenfopaecfbphgcfihbdmkec`).

## Code scanning's findings, triaged (2026-11-10)

GitHub's code scanning (CodeQL, security-and-quality) listed 99 open findings once the repository was public. No
secrets, no vulnerable dependencies. Each was read in its code; the ones that touch what ships were fixed, the rest
dismissed with the reason, so the Security tab lists only what matters.

- **A slow regex on imported themes (fixed).** The check that a theme's svg file starts with `<svg` (`theme-loader.ts`)
  was a regex with a repeated comment group; a file of a few thousand empty comments made it backtrack for minutes.
  Importing a crafted theme could freeze the import. `svgStarts` reads the start once, with the regex's rules (the
  tests run both on the same files); crafted files are refused in milliseconds.
- **`__proto__` as a data name (hardened).** Collection and item names in data sets come from Margin.app and other
  copies; `x[name] = …` with `__proto__` changes an object's prototype. `isName` and `usableKey` (`data-merge.ts`)
  refuse it in every merge (`mergeData`, `pruneTombstones`, the link's set in parts, kept tabs), and Margin.app's
  Rust and Swift merges drop it too, so all three agree (vector `09-reserved-name.json`). Only Margin.app could send
  one, over its token-protected local link.
- **Dismissed:** findings in tests and local tools (servers on 127.0.0.1, temporary files of benchmarks), test-only
  Rust (`#[cfg(test)]`'s fixed token), and false positives (an integer-checked key, Windows message constants read
  as bindings by an analysis without Windows, a promise compared with itself on purpose). `docs/` (design boards)
  isn't scanned.

## CI: the theme tests by what a change reaches, a nightly full run, timing counted in work (2026-11-10)

Each built-in theme ran the whole browser suite in two engines on every pull request, and themes keep coming. The
`changes` job's plan (`scripts/ci-plan.mts`, tested in `tests/ci-plan.test.ts`) now picks the browser jobs:

- **Every change to the extension:** every theme package checked with no browser, in `npm test` on Linux
  (`tests/security/packages.test.ts`: caps, sanitizer, the tree audit, the parts a theme needs to be switched away
  from, the first paint).
- **A theme's folder:** its own browser tests (`tests/theme/<id>.test.ts`) and its entries in the tests that loop over
  the themes, nobody else's. **The UI runtime, the host page, the harness or anything they import:** the
  theme-agnostic tests (every `tests/theme/*.test.ts` but a theme's own) against the reference theme, Arcadia
  (`MARGIN_TEST_THEMES=reference`; a file without Arcadia, `behaviors.test.ts`, takes its first). **A theme test
  itself:** that file, in every theme. **The workflow, the lockfiles, the build or the plan; nightly; by hand:**
  everything, every theme, both engines.
- **`MARGIN_TEST_THEMES`** (`tests/theme/package.ts themesInScope`), not `MARGIN_THEMES`, which adds packages to the
  security suite. Unset, every theme: `npm run gate` and local runs are unchanged.
- **End to end** only when a change reaches it (the extension, the host page, the connector, its harness and pages):
  a unit test or a theme test alone no longer starts them.
- **"At once" counted in work:** `switch-plain`'s presses must reach the overlay and Safari before the event loop's
  next turn (no timer, no write, no wait in between), not within 5 ms of wall clock, which a loaded runner missed. A
  1 ms timer in the path fails it (checked); the old bound let it pass.

## The page box keeps its walk of content-named style sheets (2026-11-10)

GitHub issue #3: every load walked every rule of every sheet to find the few the box rewrites (viewport units,
queries about the window's size); GitHub has some 38,000 rules for about 450, and `walkRules` + `readSelectors` were
two thirds of Margin's extra script there. Now what a walk finds in a file is kept (`shared/sheet-walk.ts`), and a
return visit touches only those rules.

- **Option 2 of the issue, with a day's limit.** Kept only for a file whose address names its contents
  (`contentNamed`: a hex hash of 8+ with a digit and a letter, or a Vite-style base64 one, in the path or the
  query; or an `integrity` on its `<link>`). Every other file (Wikipedia's `load.php`, `style.css?ver=6.4`) gets the
  full walk every time. Option 1 (use the cache for any file, walk again in idle time) can't be made safe on the
  load path: a file changed under its address would be wrong until the idle walk, and it saves no work. Before an
  entry is used it's checked: the rule count, the decoded size where Resource Timing gives it, and every kept rule at
  its place (its kind, and a hash of its selector and declarations, its query, or its import's address; each
  `:has()` selector as text). Anything off: the full walk, and its result replaces the entry. What no check short of
  the walk sees (a hashed file changed in place so that a rule that needed nothing now needs work, size and count
  the same) is wrong at most until the entry is a day old (`MAX_AGE_MS`): older entries aren't used.
  `tests/e2e/sheet-walk.test.ts` shows that case wrong without the age and right with it.
- **What's kept invalidates itself.** Each origin's group carries a mark: a hash of `WALK_FORMAT`, the user agent
  (the browser's version) and the text of the functions that decide what a walk finds (`hasUnits`, `asksSize`,
  `walkRules`, `visit`, `readSelectors`, …). A Margin or browser update that changes them ignores the old entries.
- **Storage.** Margin's own storage.local, never the site's: `sheetWalk:<page origin>` (read only by that origin's
  pages, so a page can only ever feed itself) and `sheetWalkIndex`. Content scripts read their origin's key at start
  on its own (not with the state, and pages never read these keys with it: `stored.ts pageKeys`, `onlyMark`, and
  core.ts/host.ts ignore their change events); the background alone writes (`keepSheetWalk`, one write at a time),
  under the origin of the page that sent it. Caps: 40 files and 64 KB per origin, 300 files and 1 MB in all, the
  least recently used origins dropped first; an entry over 24 KB isn't kept. A page gets 3 writes at most, and a
  return visit writes nothing (its group's use is noted once a day). GitHub's group: 26 files, 37 KB. A write
  reaches every open page's content script as a change event (storage.local's way), which drops it: rare (a new
  or changed file), at most 64 KB.
- **Never in the way.** The page's world asks for the kept walks as it starts; a sheet visited before they arrive
  gets the full walk as before (no sheet waits: a wait would leave its units the window's for a page script reading
  layout meanwhile). A sheet walked in full whose findings turn out to be what was kept still skips its
  `:has()` selector read (`keptHas`). No new sheet writes, no new style reads.
- **Measured** (2026-11-10, same session, `npm run bench:sites -- --sites github.com,en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser
  --runs 5`; the bench now takes `--visits first|return`; "off" is this build with `contentNamed` always false,
  i.e. the walk as on main). The box's extra over a plain load, fcp/dcl/load ms:

  | github.com | off | first visit | return visit |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Chromium | 96 / 82 / 120 | 64 / 118 / 153 | 104 / 77 / 119 |
  | WebKit | 251 / 464 / 395 | 244 / 457 / 389 | 238 / 446 / 378 |

  (Main itself, with the bench as it was, the same morning: Chromium 92 / 65 / 109, WebKit 1077 / 1150 / 1082, its
  WebKit boxed loads growing round by round with no boxed load before them; hence the same-session "off".)
  Wikipedia (no content-named files) is unchanged in both (Chromium 12–28 / 77–83 / 31–38, WebKit 80–85 / 86–91 /
  37–44). Chromium's page timings move within their noise (±30 ms); the main thread shows it.
  A/B on github.com, first visit (kept walks cleared) and return visit by turns, medians:
  | github.com, medians of 5 | first visit | return visit |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Chromium, CDP script time (all of the page's) | 517 ms | 412 ms (earlier runs: 459–467) |
  | Chromium, the box's sheet walk / :has() read | 90 / 50 ms | 37 / 0 ms (earlier runs: 59–92 / 0–3) |
  | WebKit, the box's sheet walk / :has() read | 71 / 49 ms | 24 / 0 ms |
  | WebKit, DCL / FCP | 931 / 510 ms | 896 / 457 ms |
  The layout is the same both ways: a fingerprint of every readable rule's text after the box's work matched across
  all loads, in both engines. In Chromium the storage reply comes 20–220 ms after the content script starts (the
  state's read is as slow then), so the `<head>`'s first sheets are often walked before it: what's saved there
  depends on it. In WebKit it came at ~100 ms, after every sheet. `npm run bench:box` (no content-named sheets
  there): every size within its baseline in both engines.
- **Tests.** `tests/sheet-walk.test.ts` (addresses, entries and their checks, ages, merges, caps, the background's
  writer); the box pattern `kept-sheet-walk` (both engines); `tests/e2e/sheet-walk.test.ts` and the WebKit host's
  `kept-walks` (first visit, return visit, a kept rule changed, a rule more, a change no check sees once a day old).

## The page box with classic scroll bars (2026-11-10)

GitHub issue #17: on a Mac set to always show scroll bars (or with a mouse and no trackpad: CI's Macs), a page in
the box came out a scroll bar wider than in a plain window wherever something is fixed (bars, banners, bubbles).

- **The cause.** In the box `<html>` is the containing block for what's fixed (its `transform`) and `<body>` is the
  scroller, its classic bar inside it at the box's right edge. What's fixed was laid out in `<html>`'s whole width,
  bar strip included; a window lays it out in the window less its scroll bars (and `<html>` is that wide too). The
  same along the bottom for a page wider than the box. Reproduced: Chromium 5 patterns (`#nav at 0,0,1172,57, plain
  0,0,1157,57`), the WebKit host 5 (17 px bars; `scroll-lock` among them, below).
- **The fix (`content/page/box-bars.ts`, `shared/page-box.ts barsCss`).** While `<body>`'s bars take space,
  `<html>` is narrower (shorter) by them and `<body>` reaches past it to the box's edge: its right margin less the
  bar (`box-body.ts writePadding`), its heights plus the bottom one (`bodyFitCss` `below`). So what's fixed, `<html>`,
  `document.documentElement.clientWidth` and the width `<body>` is worked out from (`whole`, a centred `<body>`) are as
  in a window, and `<body>` and its bar are where they were. Top-layer elements are placed against the box less the
  bars (`top-layer.ts`), as a window's are, and a window-rooted IntersectionObserver's `rootBounds` is too. Not
  `overflow-clip-margin` (no WebKit), not a border on `<html>` (its width, which `whole` is read from, would stay the
  bar's strip wider), not a Margin scroller around `<body>` (DECISIONS 2026-11-01). `<html>`'s `overflow: clip`
  propagates to the window (the root's overflow is the viewport's), so `<body>` sticking out of `<html>` isn't clipped,
  in either engine.
- **Measured, not guessed.** A ResizeObserver on `<body>` (a bar coming or going changes its content box), after
  layout: the browser's own `offsetWidth - clientWidth` less the borders, and the same down. Written only when a
  value changes, into a sheet of its own after the box's (`sheets.bars`), with rules about `<html>` and `<body>`
  only: Chromium styles just those two again as a bar comes or goes. What's written keeps `<body>`'s content box as it
  was, so the observer has nothing more to say in that frame (a new padding for a centred `<body>`, or `<body>`'s
  overflow, waits for the next frame: changing its size in the callback would reach the page as the observer's loop
  error). A bar on the left (right to left) is left as it is.
- **Overlay scroll bars (the default with a trackpad): nothing changes.** Every bar measures 0, the bars' sheet stays
  empty (never even replaced), the box's own sheet is byte for byte what it was, and the padding and fit sheets are
  too (unit tests). What runs is the observer and its reads of sizes after layout. `npm run bench:box`: every size
  within its baseline in both engines.
- **`overflow: scroll` on `<html>`** (springer.com's `body-clips-sideways`) shows the window's own bars at the
  window's edge, which never scrolls; Chromium's `100vw` then leaves them out, so `<html>` came out two bars narrow.
  Where bars take space (`seen`: once `<body>`'s or the window's have), the window's are hidden
  (`scrollbar-width: none` on `<html>`, which is the viewport's) and `<body>` gets `overflow: scroll` for the page's
  `scroll` (`box-locks.ts`), as a window shows its bar always. Whether the window's take space is looked at once, in
  the next frame, when the page starts saying `scroll`; with overlay bars `<body>` stays `auto` as before.
- **WebKit doesn't lay `<body>`'s children out again when its classic bar goes because its overflow turned hidden**
  (a scroll lock): they kept the bar's width free (`scroll-lock` in the host: sections 883 wide, plain 900), with or
  without the box's change; only a change of `<body>`'s own width makes it. So when a bar goes or gets thinner,
  `<body>` is a pixel narrower for one layout, within the observer's callback (an element of Margin's after it,
  `margin-relayout`, as the reads' flags), then as it was, its scroll kept. Not when one comes (WebKit lays out
  again itself then), and never on a page where no bar has taken space.
- **The cost, with classic bars only.** As the first bar shows (a page's content growing past the box), one more
  restyle and layout before that frame is painted. Chromium: nothing measurable (`bench:box` with classic bars, its
  heavy page's load to frame -6 ms against -11 overlay). WebKit restyles every element for any sheet written: +60 to
  +80 ms on the 20,000-rule bench page, +5 ms on the 2,000-rule one. The window's own layout has to lay the page out
  again as its bar shows too.
- **Tests.** `MARGIN_SCROLL_BARS` (`always` or `overlay`): `scripts/scroll-bars.mts` runs a command with Chrome for Testing's
  own `AppleShowScrollBars` set and put back after (its app domain, never the Mac's global one); the WebKit host takes
  it as its argument domain (`run.sh`: `-AppleShowScrollBars Always`, nothing written; `defaults write host …`
  worked too but left a `host.plist` behind). Both box-pattern runs check first that the browser shows the bars
  asked for. `npm run test:classic` (both engines; in `npm run gate`); CI runs the Chromium patterns with classic
  bars on the first end-to-end Mac and the host's on the macOS job, beside the runs with the runner's
  `WhenScrolling`. The rules measure the window's bars (`bars`: innerWidth less `<html>`'s clientWidth): `box-size`
  and `told-size` allow a plain window's, and a new rule, `same-bars`, holds the box to them. New pattern
  `classic-scroll-bars` (fixed bars top, bottom and corner, a percent-wide fixed bar, a centred `<body>`, a row wider
  than the box, a modal dialog). Before, with classic bars: 5 of the 22 patterns failed in Chromium, and main's build failed 8 of these 23 in the host; this
  one: all 23 pass in both engines with both settings. `tests/page-css.test.ts`: the bars' sheet empty with none,
  its rules about `<html>` and `<body>` only, the relayout's flag after `<body>`.
- **Not done.** A bar on the left for right-to-left pages; Chromium's `100vw` without the window's bar for a page
  saying `overflow-y: scroll` on `<html>` (the box keeps `100vw` the window's); for such a page, the setting changed
  in System Settings while it's open is followed only as far as `<body>`'s own bars. Needs a check in real Safari
  with "Show scroll bars: Always" (only the WebKit host and Chromium were run).

## The e2e trackpad runs on their own clock, and the start page's todos without a 5 s wait (2026-11-10)

The two flakes left in GitHub issue #13's end-to-end tests:

- **The two-finger swipe and pull to refresh (`tests/e2e/scroll.test.ts`).** The gestures read each wheel event's
  own `timeStamp` (shared/pull.ts: a gap over `GAP_MS`, 140 ms, starts a new gesture) and end on a wall-clock timer
  after the last one (content/trackpad.ts). The test sent its run with an awaited `page.mouse.wheel` per event (which
  waits for the page to handle it: ~34 ms a round trip on a fast Mac) plus 16 ms, so on a slow machine the gaps
  passed 140 ms and the gesture ended halfway. Now `wheelRun` sends the run through CDP `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`
  (`mouseWheel`), each event stamped `t0 + i × 16 ms` (`timestamp`; Chromium gives it to the page as
  `event.timeStamp`, checked) and sent on a 16 ms schedule of its own, not after the last one's answer. Still trusted
  events through Margin's capture listener; Chromium may merge two that reach the page in one frame (deltas added,
  the later stamp), as it does a trackpad's. Measured with the page's CPU slowed down (CDP
  `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate`, 20–40×): the old sending saw gaps of 146–151 ms and failed the pull test in 5 of
  7 runs; the new one saw 16 or 32 ms between stamps and passed every gesture test in 6 of 6.
  (A CPU hog of 16 busy loops on the 8-core Mac didn't reach 140 ms gaps; the throttled page did.) The tests still
  fail when the gesture logic breaks: thresholds too high fail the pull and the swipe, too low (any 20 px) fail
  "a small one" and "too small".
- **"waited 5000 ms for the launcher".** Every one in CI's logs (five runs) and in local runs, loaded or not, comes
  from the two `todo` tests of Margin's start page opened on purpose (`newtab.html#launcher`: newtab.test.ts and
  archive.test.ts), which fail on every run by a known bug (shared/view.ts `NEW_TAB_PAGE` takes no `#hash`), not
  from load: Node's spec reporter lists failing todos under "failing tests", so their 5 s timeouts read as flakes.
  The launcher tests that pass never failed in CI's logs, nor locally at four files at once beside 8–16 busy loops
  (147 of 147). The todos now wait for the overlay to have the start page in front (`startPageInFront`, ui.ts: its row,
  the New Tab row or the launcher, which come in the same draw) and then look for the launcher: they fail at once with
  "the launcher drawn over the start page". With `NEW_TAB_PAGE` taking a hash (tried, not kept), newtab.test.ts's
  todo passes that way; archive.test.ts's then fails sooner (its start page not in front after the archive button):
  the product fix is more than the pattern.

## Safari startup: current profile identities and a native splash (2026-11-10)

- **Measured in the installed app's logs.** At 12:09:55 Margin started; Safari's copies started around
  12:09:59, linked within the next ~150 ms (the handler's link reply took 156–406 ms), and the overlay
  pages drew at 12:10:01.7. Drawing did not mean showing: the restored Test A/B windows were identified
  as hidden historical copies, while their current copies remained unbound. At 11:51 the same old
  identities held blank startup covers for their full six seconds. Safari starting its extensions late
  is one part of the delay; the incorrect window identity is a separate bug that can prevent showing entirely.
- **The cause.** BrowserProfiles.browserNames deliberately retains names for historical copy IDs after a
  signing change, for data carry-over and the profile picker. The live browser.json confirms Test A and
  Test B each have an old hidden ID and a current ID linked to the same Safari profile. AX matching was
  using all those names, choosing a dictionary entry when names tied, and keeping that identity for the
  life of the window. Window matching now uses windowNames, only Safari's current mapping. Cached AX
  identities whose copy is no longer in that mapping are forgotten and read again. A mapping change
  wakes tracking and the cover loop. Two current profiles with identical names remain ambiguous instead
  of choosing one; the binder's other evidence can still identify them.
- **The startup cover is native AppKit.** “Getting things ready for you”, a secondary message and a system
  spinner draw without waiting for an extension link, theme or WebKit. Once that window's copy links,
  the message becomes “Preparing your layout…”. Reduced motion leaves the spinner still. The panel follows
  the restored window's frame as it changes and keeps the existing focus, pointer, profile and full-screen
  rules. It goes when the overlay is shown/placed, and the existing six-second limit and stalled-link
  release remain. This cannot cover a window before the helper starts Margin and Accessibility identifies it.
- **Report the front window before scanning other Spaces.** SafariAX.refresh used to hold windows it had
  already found until the private element scan finished (up to one second while Safari is busy restoring).
  It now reports known windows first and newly scanned ones afterwards; AXKnown merges both deliveries.
  The scan's limits and retry rules stay as before. The real Safari latency improvement needs a cold-launch check.
- **Diagnostics.** Each overlay records load-to-drawn milliseconds; each covered window records when its
  copy links and how long the splash lasted before the actual layout showed. No page titles or URLs added.
- **Verification.** Regression checks cover historical IDs, current matching, invalidation and relearning,
  ambiguous names and overlapping name prefixes. Native end-to-end checks render the splash off screen
  in both appearances and check layout, stage changes and focus/pointer behavior. TESTING.md has the real
  Safari cold-launch checks. Historical Safari logs were inspected; the changed build has not been
  manually verified in Safari.
- **Browser verification:** `npm test`: 1,017 passed. `npm run test:e2e`: the final run passed all 149;
  the first run passed 148 and failed the archive/palette restore (also intermittent in isolated repeats,
  with no extension or browser-test changes kept). Native checks passed 2,070 on the full randomized run,
  then 2,071 after the scan-delivery regression was added (WINDOW_RUNS=50, VISIBLE_RUNS=80); all 491 native
  end-to-end checks passed, including the splash's two appearances. The app, handler and helper type-check
  without compiler warnings.

## The launch splash belongs to a temporary helper process (2026-11-10)

- **Keep the idle saving.** The request was a splash from margin-helper without keeping the full app at login
  or paying for windows in the resident watcher. AppKit's window connection keeps tens of MB in a process even
  after its panels go. The login helper therefore never creates NSApplication or a window: its existing
  NSWorkspace observation stays event-driven, with no poll. A recently launched supported browser, while
  Margin.app is not running, starts the app and a `--splash <browser pid>` child of the helper in parallel.
  An older browser already open as the helper starts gets no launch card; an app already running gets no child.
- **The child alone draws.** A small native “Getting things ready for you” card, ordered just above that browser's
  first on-screen window, follows its bounds without taking the keyboard, showing a Dock icon or taking clicks.
  Window metadata only: no title, profile, Accessibility, page, WebKit or network. It reads at 10 Hz for at most
  six seconds, exits on browser quit, and exits if the person switches away after it shows. This is deliberately
  a passive launch card before a profile can be identified, not the app's profile-specific full-window cover.
- **The app takes over.** Once a native startup cover or on-screen overlay has been ordered over that browser,
  the app sends `com.unibox.margin.startup.ready`, scoped to its pid and actual window number. A different
  window on a second display cannot dismiss the card. Merely connecting the extension or loading
  the overlay page doesn't count. The child asks `startup.query` after subscribing: if the app drew before the
  child started, the answer dismisses it too. A window placed invisibly in another Space doesn't end the card.
  These are cosmetic notifications with no data or privileges; a matching notification can only dismiss a card.
- **Measured in one session, optimized builds, off-screen stand-in browser.** Original helper after asking for
  an app: 10,944 KB resident; new helper afterwards: 11,472 KB (about 0.5 MiB more). New helper before a browser:
  8,992 KB; during the splash: 11,456 KB. No CPU time gained during the one-second idle sample. The temporary
  child used 70,528 KB including its test snapshot, drew in 200 ms after its mode started, and exited on handoff
  at 351 ms; a child starting after the ready event exited via the query at 115 ms. These are fixture measurements,
  not a real Safari cold-launch benchmark. The temporary ~69 MiB UI cost is released with the child; it isn't
  added to the always-running helper. Main app startup and its existing idle quit are unchanged.
- **Updates.** safari.sh now restarts an already loaded login agent after replacing the installed app, so an
  old resident helper doesn't keep running old code until next login. It doesn't load or enable a disabled agent.
- **Tests.** Real helper processes over an off-screen fake browser: launch, arguments, idle CPU and resident
  memory before/during/after, early handoff, late-listener recovery, pid isolation, six-second timeout, browser
  quit. Tests refuse an on-screen frame. The app's actual responder is exercised in its native end-to-end run.
  Two initially parallel test commands shared fixture files and interfered; those results were discarded.
  Helper fixture folders and browser IDs are now unique per run, and the clean helper run passed every check.
  `npm test`: 1,017 passed; `npm run test:e2e`: 149 passed; native logic: 2,071 passed; native end-to-end: 496 passed
  (five new handoff checks). The installed Safari launch and Space transitions still need manual verification.

  Space preview after a three-finger upward swipe. The own-Space policy used `.managed`, which explicitly
  opts the transparent Margin panel into Mission Control's independent window arrangement. Its pointer
  catcher and edge guard inherited the same policy. Staying in the same Space does not combine those
  windows into the browser's document.
- **Small native policy change.** Own-Space overlays now use `.stationary, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .ignoresCycle`.
  They still belong to one Space (no `.canJoinAllSpaces`), with placement verified by the existing bridge,
  and retain their normal window level. All three native layers receive the same policy. The fallback
  that joins all Spaces already used stationary and is unchanged. No timers, gesture detection, capture,
  screenshots, new windows, reloads or helper changes. The ordinary tracking and rendering paths stay as before.

  as remaining visible without being affected by Mission Control, and transient as hiding in Mission Control.
  Managed, transient and stationary are alternatives; they are not combined. The regression checks the actual
  AppKit policies on both layouts and all their helper panels, alongside the existing repeated Space visits,
  no-reload/no-extra-move checks, conservative missing-read checks, and refused-placement backoff.

off-screen, two-process probe and its result excerpt. The same-process public and private controls
establish relationships. The cross-process calls, in both ownership directions and through AppKit's
transaction variants, do not: readback stays separate and the owned child's parent ID stays zero.
Some calls still return zero. No private grouping implementation is enabled in Margin on that evidence.
The probe's final REA Evidence ID is `ev_0672265891a11f6159ac261b1a24186944f242c1c78fe9d9d2b8d4b42e9b830f`.

code was ruled out. The ineffective stationary change and its policy-only regression are removed; the

## Margin 2: saved-tab navigation, dedicated Settings and Mission Control fallback (2026-11-10)

The user chose hiding Margin in Mission Control after confirming the detached/scaled appearance happens
only in its previews. All three overlay layers now use AppKit's `transient` policy, including the
all-Spaces fallback, in place of `managed`/`stationary`. Apple's collection-behavior documentation says
transient windows hide in Mission Control. The existing windows, WebViews, browser page geometry,
Space placement and readiness/missing-read protections remain. No gesture observer, polling, new
renderer, screenshot cache or helper work is added. The browser's page insets intentionally stay
prepared; this does not promise a full-width, reflowed Safari thumbnail. A real Mission Control
entry/exit/reversal observation remains necessary because live desktop capture failed previously.

Two navigation causes were reproduced. The shared key cycle explicitly excluded kept rows; its
background and overlay pick also required integer browser IDs. Saved IDs now participate in the same
sidebar order and optimistic selection, including pinned URLs with a saved tab. Clicks, keys and
space restore share the kept-tab reopen path, preserving Margin identity, place and scroll metadata.
The key chain resolves that identity after the new browser ID arrives. Creation/activation before the
identity link cannot prematurely clear its highlight; only the chosen missing page opens. The
existing one-switch/latest-waiting behavior stays.

Space restore formerly tried all open pages before kept tabs, including an internal launcher, and
then reopened the first kept row rather than the last-used tab. It now compares real open and saved
records by recency. Saved `wasActive` breaks a tie (activating a tab can stamp both it and the one left
at the same millisecond). The app data's additive `selected` field preserves that information through
a wiped extension cache; older records default false. The separate closed-profile window restore
uses the same kept-tab tie break. An already shown real tab of the requested space stays shown.

Safari resync and reclaim retain known Margin `order` values instead of deriving a new sidebar order
from Safari's strip. Explicit sidebar drags write a Margin place. After ordinary selection, only a
cached order mismatch schedules a physical position repair: a linear scan on the selection path, no
additional browser call when ordered, no waiting before activation, at most one repair per window,
latest target retained while one is running. No speculative tab loads or background reordering loop.

Internal start/new-tab anchors are omitted from sidebar and palette tab results even when inactive;
new-tab keys still use the palette and first/empty windows retain their necessary browser anchor.
Settings is a named page/row, opened directly by the palette's Settings action or `margin://settings`
in Margin's fields, reusing an existing page per window and coalescing concurrent opens. It uses the

## The slot: the browser's own window sized to the page, in place of the page box (2026-11-15)

Asked by Tirth on 2026-11-15, after two days of tests outside the repo: build the slot into Margin itself and do the rest of the testing here.

**What it is.** Every full-screen Space lays its window out in a tile and can reserve room at its edges (`SLSSpaceSetEdgeReservation`, `docs/PRIVATE-APIS.md` rows 21-22). With the layout's insets reserved, macOS lays the tile out again and the browser sizes its own full-screen window to what's left. The page is then the whole window: nothing is added to it, where the page box sizes the page inside a full-size window (its cost per page is in "What the box costs, measured").

**Off by default.** `defaults write com.unibox.margin MarginNativeSlot -bool YES` turns it on. Off, no keeper is made and every window keeps the page box exactly as before. It stays off until it has been checked in real Safari (`TESTING.md`, "The slot").

**How it's built (branch `feat/native-slot`).**
- *One seam.* `Shell.layoutChanged` is where a window's layout goes to its copy. For a full-screen window drawn over whole, the layout's insets are reserved in its Space, and its copy is sent a layout with no insets: the extension's existing "no box" path, first paint included. The extension is not changed. Anything else gets the layout as before.
- *The keeper* (`Slot.swift`). One slot per browser window: its Space, its full frame, the edges, whether it landed. Every reservation is verified against the window's own bounds within 1.5 s, sent once more, then given back; that window keeps the page box for the session, and two windows failing in a row turn the slot off for the session.
- *The model.* The rest of the shell works on windows that fill their display (overlay frames, the planner and placer, the handoff's readiness, the covers). Rewriting all of that for a smaller window was the risky way. Instead every read of the window server goes through `SlotWindows`, which gives a slotted window at the bounds it would have with nothing reserved; the copy's own bounds for that window and the model-geometry read are put in the same terms. With no slot set, it is the identity.
- *A steady full frame.* While a window is resizing into its slot, the model gives its recorded full frame, not one worked out from bounds in motion: the overlay must not be sized, and its layout measured, against a moving window.
- *Giving it back.* A reservation outlives the process that set it, unlike everything else Margin sets through private calls. So: zeros when the window leaves full screen, when its page takes the screen (a video in full screen should fill the display), when it's parked, when no linked window is bound to it for longer than a dropped link is kept, when the displays change, and at quit; a marker (`slots.json`: Space numbers and a pid) read at the next launch after a crash, whether or not the setting is still on; and a Space found already reserved is given back before it's used.
- *macOS only.* The Rust core (Windows) isn't touched.

**Verified.** The launch check and wrappers against fake functions, the keeper against a stand-in for the Spaces, and the whole seam through the real shell and overlay with a stand-in that plays the window manager (`tools/app-tests/e2e-slot.swift`): the layout reserved, no insets sent, the overlay kept over the whole display, the copy's smaller bounds still bound, out of full screen and back, a window that won't take the slot given the page box, quit. The existing unit and end-to-end checks pass unchanged with the setting off.

**Not verified: anything in real Safari, Chrome or Edge.** The private call itself was only run from test code outside the repo (macOS 27.2.1, 26B131: Safari, Chrome for Testing, Maps and others), not from this code.

**Known gaps, for the Safari check to judge.**
- The page's corners are square (the browser's window is), where the page box rounds them.
- When the slot is first taken, the copy is told to drop the box at the same moment the window starts to shrink: the page may be seen to reflow once.
- Safari's own full-screen title strip still slides over the top of the page when the menu bar is revealed, as in plain full-screen Safari today.
- (Fixed 2026-11-15, found in Tirth's own Safari the first time the slot was on.) The full-screen toolbar is a window of Safari's own, laid out with the tile: with a slot it has the slot's left edge and width and sits the top's reservation lower (hidden at y −11 with 8 reserved, not −19). Left at its real bounds beside its window's model frame, it wasn't found as the toolbar and, hidden, overlapped the frame's top by 8 pt, so the exact stacking check read it as a foreign window between Margin's layout and the page: the profile switch's live cover never reached R4, timed out after 7 s and backed the switch out (`live cover stack blocked`, 10:54). The keeper's model now puts a slotted window's toolbar where it would be with nothing reserved, by the same rule the shell knows a toolbar by; `slot-tests.swift` has the window list of that session, failing first.
- A window that loses its binding while slotted is bound again only after its slot is given back (about 6 s).
- The edge stop keeps its fence at the display's left edge, not the window's.
- Other apps as tabs, Margin in a window, and the Mission Control and outside-open questions from the tests are later stages, not started here.

## Opening Margin: its browser's window comes up inside it (2026-11-15)

Asked by Tirth on 2026-11-15, on trying the slot's build: Margin should be what is opened, with the browser coming up inside it, as the test kit did with its apps, and not Margin waiting for Safari to be opened and put in full screen by hand.

**What it is.** Opened by hand, or opened again while it runs (Spotlight, Finder, a kept Dock icon), Margin.app asks its shell to `enter` (`ShellEnter.swift`) in place of showing the set-up window. The shell picks the window the person last used among the linked copies' windows (`EnterPick`: the focused one, then the one focused last, then the one made last; a minimized one only when there's no other; never a parked one), asks its copy for it in full screen and in front with the request the profile switch already sends (`focusWindow`), and brings its browser to the front. From there nothing is new: the overlay over the full-screen window, its page in the slot or the page box.

**No window to open into.** The browser is opened once through `NSWorkspace` (started if it isn't running; one running with no window makes one): a linked one, else one that's running, else the one Margin was last linked with (`MarginLastBrowser`, written at each link; Safari the first time). Its copy's link and its window are then waited for, 15 s at most. Nothing by then, the app is told why and shows its set-up window, which is where a missing extension is seen.

**The set-up window** is still there: when the opening fails, when Margin is opened holding Option, and when it's already open.

**The setting.** On with the slot (`MarginNativeSlot`), since the two together are the Margin Tirth asked for; `MarginOpensBrowser` turns it on or off by itself. Off, opening Margin shows the set-up window exactly as before.

**Mine, not asked:** which window (the last used), the Option key for the set-up window, the 15 s, and that the browser keeps its own Dock icon and its name in Mission Control for now. Hiding those needs the browser started by Margin without a Dock icon, which the test kit did for other apps and nobody has tried with a browser (an AppKit app started that way could not go into full screen in the kit: `multi-app` notes); it is its own step.

**Verified.** `enter-tests.swift` (18 checks: the window and the browser chosen) and `e2e-enter.swift` (15 checks through the real link and shell against the fake extension, with a recorder in place of `NSWorkspace`): one browser opened once and waited for, the window asked for once in full screen, two asks at once one request, a failure only after the wait, quitting ends one under way.

**Not verified.** Anything with a real browser (`TESTING.md`, "Opening Margin"): that `focusWindow` with full screen brings a Desktop window of a browser that isn't in front into full screen and forward, how long a cold Safari takes to link, and what the first seconds look like (the helper's launch card, the window's own full-screen animation).

**What Tirth's first try showed (2026-11-15, 10:51 to 10:54, the log).** The slot lands in real Safari: 25 ms for the first reservation, 12 to 28 ms for each sidebar hide and show, 67 ms for a new full-screen window. A switch to a space in another profile failed (the toolbar, above, since fixed and not yet tried again). And the build they were trying still opened the set-up window when Margin was opened, which is what this section answers.

**Not done yet (the rest of what was asked).** Other apps as items in the sidebar that open in the page's place; Margin's own name on the Dock, the menu bar and Mission Control in place of the browser's; the page box removed once the slot has held up.

## Margin.app owns the spaces: the library (2026-11-15)

Phase 1 of `docs/MARGIN-APP.md`: with `MarginHosted` on (`defaults write com.unibox.margin MarginHosted -bool YES`, read in `Shell.forApp` into `Shell.Options.hosted`), the app keeps the person's spaces, pins, folders and Margin tabs ("items") itself, in one data set of its own, instead of each profile's copy keeping its own. Off (the default), nothing of it runs: no file is read or made, and every profile's copy keeps its spaces exactly as before.

**Where.** `data/app/set.json` and `data/app/items/<collection>.json` beside the profiles' sets (`DataStore` with `flat: true`: the same files, backups, atomic writes and merge rules, one set). Collections: `spaces` (`name`, `emoji`, `color`, `order`, `browser`, `profile`: the Safari profile its new web items open in, null for the default), `pins`, `folders`, `tabs` (the items), `archive`, `windows` (each Margin window's space), `imports` (the import's marker).

**Items have a target.** `{ kind: 'web', browser: 'safari', profile }` or `{ kind: 'app', bundleId, name }`, on every item, pin and archive entry, so a space can mix pages of several Safari profiles and Mac apps. An app item's address is `app://<bundleId>`: the model matches by address, and only `http(s)` pages are ever archived, so closing an app forgets it.

**The library's rules are margin-core's** (since 2026-11-24, docs/CORE-REFACTOR.md step 4; this replaces 2026-11-15's "one copy of the rules: the TypeScript model in JavaScriptCore, not a Swift port"). One copy still: the rules are app/shared/core/src/library, a function-by-function port of `app/shared/library/library.ts` over `extension/state/model.ts` (with pinned-rules.ts, air-traffic.ts, front-item.ts), which Margin.app runs through margin-ffi and the Windows shell runs as it is, with no JavaScript engine (Tirth, 2026-11-22: the rules go into the core once the hosted design is the only one coming; no WebAssembly). The TS stays only as the shared vectors' reference (tests/fixtures/library: the TS tests' calls, generated sequences, the edges as JavaScriptCore answers them, every step checked against the core) and as the extension's own rules while the browsers' copies own their spaces; it's built into nothing. The merge, the files and the times are the core's store's (data/library.rs, data/store.rs), as they are for the profiles. Until step 4: `scripts/build.ts` bundled library.ts as `dist/app/library.js` and `LibraryRules.swift` ran it in a `JSContext`, JSON in and out (the reasons then: one copy of the subtle rules, already tested; JavaScriptCore a system framework). What the move decided (Tirth's answers): ICU collation exact through the system's sorter, ties by the ids' order, a cut through an emoji drops the broken half, addresses parsed as the browsers do, the no-rules fallback gone.

**Times.** The rules give untimed values; the store stamps each (`Library.apply` until step 4, data/library.rs since) at now, or just after the item's own time when the clock went back, and merges them like any change.

**The import (decided by Tirth).** The first time the library opens with `MarginHosted` on, every profile's set the app keeps (every browser's) is imported once (`Library.importOnce`): spaces with the profile as their own, pins, folders, every Margin tab (open or kept) as a web item in that profile, and the archive. Ids are namespaced, `<browser>:<profile>:<id>` (an item: `t-` and a hash of the same, since the model and UI take only `t-` ids for tabs), so two profiles' `personal` stay two spaces. The order is `browser.json`'s through `BrowserProfiles.resolve` (the slots rule), read only; a forgotten profile's spaces are imported too, after the others. The marker (`imports.done`: when, which sets, counts) is saved with what it brought, and `set.json` is written last, so a crash before it reruns the import, which gives the same ids. Nothing in the profiles' files is written or deleted (checked file by file). Settings, theme settings and site icons are not imported: they stay each profile's for now.

**The read API and actions** (`Library.swift`): `snapshot()` (the UI's stored-values shape: `spaces`, `pins`, `folders`, `archive`, `openTabs.keptTabs` with each item's target, `library: { v, imported }`, for `ui/host-app.ts` with minimal change), `spaces()`, `items(space:)`, `target(ofItem:)`, `space(ofWindow:)`, `observe(_:)`. `perform(action, payload)` takes the UI's names and payloads: setSpace, createSpace, renameSpace, deleteSpace, orderSpaces, moveTabToSpace, moveTab, pinTab, unpin, openPin, movePin, createFolder, renameFolder, setFolderOpen, deleteFolder, moveFolder, activateTab, newTab, closeTab, clearToday, restoreArchive; and the hosting's own: addItem, updateItem, itemClosed, removeItem, setSpaceProfile, forgetWindow. Anything else is refused (`unsupported`: updateSettings, the theme and history actions stay the copy's).

**What needs a browser or an app is a request, not done here.** activateTab, newTab, closeTab, setSpace, openPin, unpin, clearToday and restoreArchive change the library's own data (the item made, used, archived; the window's space) and return a request with the item, its address and its target resolved: recorded (`Library.requests`, the last 100) and given to `Library.delegate` (`LibraryDelegate`), which the hosting phase implements. Mine, not asked: the library makes the item for newTab and archives it for closeTab itself (it's the source of truth for Margin tabs now), so a page Safari fails to open is the hosting's to remove (`removeItem`); a pinned item becomes the pin, as a kept tab does in the extension.

**Not done here:** any window, hosting or palette; settings in the library; profiles that appear after the import; an empty library (no profile sets) stays empty, for the create-spaces step of the window phase.

**Verified.** `tests/library.test.ts` (9 tests: every action, the cascade, the requests, the snapshot drawn by `shared/view.ts sidebar`, the import's namespacing, order and rerun) and `library-tests.swift` in `tools/app-tests/run.sh unit` (the bundle in JavaScriptCore, the flat files read back, times after a clock that went back, the delegate, observers, the import from stand-in profile sets and `browser.json` in a temporary folder with the profiles' files unchanged, and the shell: off makes nothing, on opens and imports).

## The host engine: other apps' windows in Margin's page area (2026-11-15)

Phase 3 of `docs/MARGIN-APP.md`, built on `feat/hosted-engine` (`app/platforms/macos/shell/Host*.swift`, `ShellHost.swift`, `private/HostCalls.swift`).

**Off by default.** `defaults write com.unibox.margin MarginHosted -bool YES` (`Shell.Options.hosted`). Off, nothing of it runs except a crashed run's marker being cleaned up. The shell still has to wire it to Margin's own window (phase 2): `open(app:in:marginWindow:marginSpace:)` with the page area in top-left (window-server) coordinates, `requestSafariWindow` / `closeSafariWindow` to the extension's window requests, `poll()` on the shell's poll.

**How it's built.** A state machine (`HostEngine`) over one seam (`HostSystem`: the real one in `HostSystem.swift`, a stand-in window manager in `tests/host-tests.swift`), every operation one at a time. Showing a host, under the freeze and each step verified and timed in the log: launch with no Dock icon (an app already running that Margin didn't start is refused; a running Safari gets a window of Margin's own from its extension, never a restart) → its first window → AXFullScreen, macOS's jump to the new Space undone → Safari's sidebar hidden (a window Margin may touch) → the one shown before parked and taken out of full screen in its private Space (only two tiles in Margin's Space) → the tile moved into Margin's Space → the emptied Space destroyed by the bridge, Margin's Space made current first → the page area's edges and tile spacing reserved until the window's bounds are the page area within 1 pt.

**Fallbacks.** A failed step backs the window out of full screen (its Space goes), destroys an emptied Space or keeps it to try again (`leftSpaces`, marker, `poll`, quit, recovery), quits an app started for that open, and shows the previous host again when it had already been parked. Placement that can't be reached is said and the window stays shown.

**Decided here, for the on-screen check to judge.** The page area's top and bottom reservations apply to the whole Space, so Margin's own tile is as tall as the page area; the left edge stays Margin's (its tile flush left), the gap after its tile is the tile spacing. A Safari sidebar whose state doesn't read (another language, its closed title not learned) is pressed once only when the window doesn't fit, and pressed back if it still doesn't. An app that doesn't quit when asked (unsaved work) is left running with its window on the Desktop, and stays in the marker.

**Verified.** Unit checks against the stand-in (launch to shown, a failure at every step leaving nothing, switching and parking, quit order, recovery, outside opens, Safari's paths) and the private calls' check against a fake resolver. **Not verified: anything on the real screen.**

**Safari's window without Accessibility (2026-11-15, after the on-screen run).** Hosting an app Margin starts (TestPane) worked end to end on the real Mac; a web item in the person's running Safari failed at the window step: the window its copy made (`newWindow`) opened on the Desktop (a normal window can't open in Margin's full-screen Space), and Accessibility lists only the current Space's windows (0 of Safari's 7 listed while another Space was current), so it was never found, and the failure left that window open, in no Space. Now, for a window a copy made (the engine keeps the copy's id for it): it's found by the window server (`HostSystem.serverWindows`, CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo on every Space: a layer-0 window of Safari's pid, at least 200×200, not there before the ask; of several, the one at the bounds the copy answered; still none or several told apart by nothing: the step fails). Full screen and back go through its copy (`safariFullScreen` → `setWindowState { fullscreen, focused, notAfter }` / `normal`), asked beside the wait so macOS's jump is undone as soon as the window server shows the new type-4 Space; done is read by the window server (`spaces`, `spaceType`), not AXFullScreen. Its sidebar: Safari's main window (Accessibility) is read before the tile and, unread there, again once its tile is in Margin's Space; still unread or another window, the sidebar is left and said, never pressed blindly. Every failure after the ask closes that window by its copy (`closeSafariWindow(profile, id)`, before a Safari Margin started is quit); a close the window server doesn't confirm puts it in the marker (`leftSafariWindows`, with Safari's pid and launch time), closed by its copy from the poll, at quit or at the next launch's recovery (a window of another Safari launch is forgotten, never closed). Apps' windows: Accessibility, as before. The engine's existing `windows`/`setFullScreen` through Accessibility (`HostAX`) and the shell's window binder (off while hosted) aren't used for it. **Not verified on the real screen yet.**

## Margin as the app: the parts joined (2026-11-15)

Asked by Tirth on 2026-11-15: open Margin as an app; the first time it asks for spaces (existing ones imported); ⌘T and a search opens Safari inside Margin's page area with no Safari toolbar, Dock icon or Mission Control entry; the palette finds any installed app and opens it the same way. The four parts (the library, Margin's window, installed apps, the host engine) are joined on `feat/hosted-glue`, all behind `MarginHosted`; off, nothing changes.

**How it's joined** (`HostedSession.swift`, `ShellHostedGlue.swift`).
- *The windows draw the library* (`LibraryWindowSource`): its snapshot, with the items that have a page (hosted, or a tab of a hosted Safari window) as open tabs of the Margin window hosting them, numbered for the UI (it takes only numbers for open tabs; the session maps them back), the one shown active, so the sidebar highlights it. Settings, theme settings and site icons are still a profile's, read only, kept in memory (the earlier stand-in, `DataSetWindowSource`, which is also the fallback when the library's rules don't load). A search typed in the palette becomes a web item at the engine Safari searches with (as the copy learned it, else Google's).
- *The library's requests are the session's*, one at a time: an app item opened by the engine (`.app(bundleId)`) the first time, shown after, closed by it; a web item in Safari: one hosted window per Safari profile in use, made by that profile's copy (`newWindow`, asked by the engine only once the copy has linked: `HostEngine.safariLinked`, so windows a Safari just started restores are never taken for Margin's), shown by the engine, the item a tab of it (`hostShow`); two web items of one profile are a tab switch only. Closed: `hostClose`, the engine's close. The engine's events (an app quit, a window gone) take the items' pages away.
- *A palette pick* (`app.open`): the window's space's item for that app, else a new one (`addItem`), then shown. Safari picked: a new web item (a blank page) in the space's profile. Chrome or Edge picked: logged, nothing done. A web item's profile: its own, else the default profile's copy (`s-default`), else the first Safari copy linked.
- *Margin's window while hosting* (v1 rule, mine): taken to full screen first (the tiles need its own Space; windowed hosting is a later phase), its page told `pageOutside` (the UI then keeps the sidebar docked: there's no page to give room to) and nothing passes through it (`setHosting`), and it becomes the sidebar's tile only as the hosted window's tile comes into its Space (`HostEngine.willTile`: alone in its Space a narrow window would stand in its middle while Safari starts): its content's max width is then the page's left inset (the theme's sidebar with its margins). The engine's placing reads Margin's tile again for a moment while it's laid out at that width. The page area, given to the engine, is worked out from the tiles: the display's full-screen area (below the camera housing) less Margin's tile, less the theme's top, bottom and right insets (the right one as last measured with room for a page; in the tile there's none to measure), which the engine reserves at the Space's edges. A change (the sidebar's width, another theme) goes to `pageRectChanged`. Nothing hosted any more: the whole width again.
- *The overlay path is off* with `MarginHosted`: the shell's read of the window server makes no binding, overlay, `drawn` or layout for any browser window (`hostedTrack`: the host's poll instead); the slot and opening the browser (ShellEnter) are off too. The copies stay linked as the tabs' drivers.
- *The first run* with nothing to import: one space made (Personal) and opened in the UI's own space editor once the window's page is drawn (`edit-space`), for the person to name; the UI has no create-spaces flow of its own, so this is the minimal one. Imported spaces come as before (the library's import).

**Mine, not asked:** full screen first; the sidebar always docked while hosting (Toggle Sidebar changes only the setting until hosting ends); one Margin window hosts at a time (the engine has one page area); Safari picked = a blank web item; the search engine as learned; a blank-page item is kept like any.
